subtopic: CONTINUATION OF PROGRAM OF SMALL POST OFFICE CONSTRUCTION
CONTINUATION OF PROGRAM OF SMALL POST OFFICE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on June 10, 1963 and again on October 14, 1963, the Minister of Labour informed the house that it was the government's intention to supplement the federal government winter construction program in order to create greater employment opportunities during the winter in designated areas. The supplementary construction program included a number of small post office buildings.
On April 15 of this year, in reply to a question, the Minister of Public Works stated 20220-484J
that all the buildings originally scheduled under this special program had not been undertaken because of site problems and cost and staff limitations.
I should now like to inform the house that it is the intention of the government to continue the special program consisting of those locations in certain designated areas and areas of high winter unemployment that, while included in the original listings, it was not possible to complete during the last winter season. Approximately 185 locations will be involved as compared with 103 last year.
It must be appreciated, however, that although yesterday I passed the names on to my colleague the Minister of Public Works for construction, it will be subject to his being able to make satisfactory arrangements with respect to the acquisition of suitable sites and to obtain tenders reasonable in cost. One reason names are being forwarded at this time is to afford ample opportunity to acquire suitable sites well in advance of the winter season.

subsubtopic: LEVELS OF RADIOACTIVITY AMONG CANADIAN ESKIMOS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that Canada has the highest rate of radioactive fall-out in the world, and in view of the dangerously high levels of radioactive caesium 137 recently found in Alaskan Eskimos, has the government considered testing Canadian Eskimos for similar danger?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: LEVELS OF RADIOACTIVITY AMONG CANADIAN ESKIMOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the radiation protection division of our department has been making a special study of the problem in Canadian Eskimos in co-operation with the northern health services of the department and with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We published preliminary reports in the October, 1963 and April, 1964 issues of our monthly publication "Data From Radiation Protection Programs". These reports include data on caesium 137 content of samples of caribou and reindeer meat and of urine samples obtained from residents in the north whose diet contains appreciable quantities of caribou meat.
This data indicates that ceasium 137 levels are higher for persons who eat caribou meat than for the general population. However, preliminary estimates of the total amount of caesium 137 in the bodies of these people, based on the amounts measured in the urine specimens, lead to the conclusion that in general the maximum permissible body burden of caesium 137 has not been reached. The highest levels noted are slightly below the amount recognized as permissible for continuous lifetime exposure. Levels are expected, I am very pleased to be able to say, to show a gradual decrease provided, of course, that nuclear testing is not resumed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this question is supplementary to one asked yesterday by the hon. member for Royal addressed to the President of the Privy Council. I have no responsibility in this regard as a member of treasury board, but in my capacity as one of the commissioners of internal economy I do have knowledge of what is happening.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO HOLIDAYS FOR STAFF
speechtext: In view of the fact that this matter is receiving consideration by the body of which the minister is a member, will he take note of the fact that both in Ontario and in Canada there are laws requiring that there be annual holidays; and in view of the fact that many members of our staff have been working for over a year without holidays should not one or the other of these laws be observed?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO HOLIDAYS FOR STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the desire is to have better laws for our staff than are ordinarily applicable in either of the jurisdictions to which the hon. member has referred. However, the problem is not just as simple as the hon. member has stated it. It is a little more complicated. Parts of the staff have been receiving regular holidays in the usual way. There is no question so far as they are concerned. With regard to other


parts of the staff, the nature of their duties is such that they are very closely related to the actual sessions of the House of Commons, and a problem arises since these employees were all hired on the basis that they would not have holidays while the house was in session.
The difficulty has arisen because of the fact that due to the situation this year the normal policy or practice no longer was practicable. The problem is to find a method that will fully and adequately provide for the situation bearing in mind the former practice and which will not result, of course, in a cutting off of the services necessary for the functioning of the house while it is in session. It is a rather complicated matter, but it is receiving very close attention.

I should like to begin, Mr. Chairman, by saying a few things about the current employment situation. During the past year hon. members will be glad to learn that employment has shown a marked increase while unemployment has registered a noticeable de-ciine. Improvement in the employment situation was particularly marked during the first half of 1964. Manufacturing employment showed great strength, a larger than seasonal increase being recorded during recent months. Construction employment held up better than usual last winter, but more recently it has shown less buoyancy than last year. Government measures to stimulate house building activity during winter months have helped to reduce the incidents of seasonal unemployment.
Between September, 1963 and February, 1964, the seasonal high and low points for the year, the unemployment total increased by some 217,000. The average seasonal swing over this period during the past five years was 322,000, so we conclude that the seasonal impact of our special winter employment program has been in the vicinity of 100,000 jobs. While construction employment is currently at somewhat lower levels than last year, the prospects for the coming months are very good. Housing starts are once again running above last year after registering a decline in May following an unusually strong first quarter. Non-residential construction can be expected to show more buoyancy during the second half of this year.
Total employment in the second quarter of 1964 averaged 261,000 higher than in the corresponding period last year. This represents a gain of 4.1 per cent, which was a substantially greater rate of advance than in any recent year. Unemployment has remained at a relatively high level even though more new jobs were created during the past year than in any previous year, with the labour force increasing by some 217,000 between the second quarter of 1963 and the second quarter of 1964. The net decrease in unemployment over the year was about 45,000.
The rate of labour force growth was well above the long term average. A little over one third of the increase in the labour force over the past year was made up by the addition to the labour force of younger workers under the age of 25 years, while almost all the remainder of the increase in the growth of the labour force was made up of women between the ages of 25 and 44 years. The comparatively large number of young workers added to the labour force was the result in

part of the population increase, but there were also changes, and significant changes, in the pattern of labour force participation amongst young people in the community.
Among the more encouraging developments of the past year was the improvement in manufacturing. In the second quarter of 1964 manufacturing employment averaged approximately 90,000 higher than the corresponding period in 1963, and almost all parts of manufacturing contributed to the advance in output and in employment during the past year. Thus far in 1964 the most marked improvement in employment has been in durable goods. The service producing industries have been expanding at an accelerated rate during the past year. During 1962 and the early part of 1963 they experienced a relatively slow rate of growth. Since the beginning of this year service employment has been running well above 100,000 higher than last year. The increase in numbers has been constantly in excess of 40,000.
Despite the impressive decrease in unemployment during the past year, Mr. Chairman, in many parts of the country it is still relatively high. In July the unemployment rates varied from 2.2 per cent on the prairies to 5.1 per cent in Quebec. The disparity was somewhat less marked than a year ago. In July, 1963 unemployment rates varied from 2.4 per cent on the prairies to 5.7 per cent in Quebec. Hon. members will be interested in noting the duration of the unemployment of those currently unemployed. Of the 265,000 unemployed in July, three quarters of the total were unemployed for three months or less. The remaining 60,000 had been seeking work for four months or more. This group accounted for a smaller proportion of the total than a year ago. The shortages of certain skilled and semi-skilled workers were becoming fairly widespread in Ontario and Quebec. During the second quarter tool and diemakers, machinists, welders, electricians and loggers were in very short supply in a number of areas. Engineers, draftsmen and miners were also reported to be in short supply in certain parts of Canada.
Turning now, Mr. Chairman, to our specific activities for the current fiscal year, the committee will be asked to provide $228,079,800 in the main estimates and $263,004 in supplementary estimates (A). Of this total of $228,342,804, and amount of $114,491,504 is required by the Department of Labour proper and $113,851,300 for the unemployment insurance commission. This represents a reduction of $105,786,850 from moneys totalling

$334 million made available in the fiscal year
1963-	64.
To account for this substantial decrease I should explain that in the main estimates for
1964-	65 no provision has been made for the continuation during the coming winter of incentive programs to reduce seasonal employment, for which over $55 million was provided in the 1963-64 estimates. There is also a substantial reduction, approximately $62 million, in our anticipated need this year in meeting our commitments for training facilities under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. This is offset somewhat by increased provision for the operating aspects of the training program. There is also an increase of over $8 million for the operations of the unemployment insurance commission.
At this point I should like to assure the committee that although no provision is being made in these main estimates for our winter works incentive program, it is the government's intention, as already announced, to continue it during the coming winter, and money provisions will be made in supplementary estimates at a later date.
As hon. members will have observed, one of the items in the supplementary estimates provides authority for the transfer of payments connected with the operation of the national employment service insurance commission to the Department of Labour, and for the transfer of the duties, powers and functions related to this service. This transfer, which was recommended by the Gill committee, has been widely endorsed by national employer and labour organizations, as well as by others.
Hon. members will note that provision of funds for the economics and research branch of the department is also included under the principal vote in the estimates, and I would like to say a word or two about the activities of this important branch of the Department of Labour. As the central federal agency for economic and social analyses and research in the labour field, this branch conducts on a continuing basis studies of employment and unemployment, skilled and professional manpower resources, wages and working conditions, union organization and collective bargaining. The results of these studies are made available not only to the federal government but also to labour and management, to international agencies and to the general public through the Labour Gazette and various regular and special reports issued by the branch.

I would like to mention a few of the branch's specific activities over the past year. Studies on seasonal unemployment were given further attention during the year. An important part of this work was concerned with assessing the effectiveness of the winter house building incentive program as a means of reducing seasonal unemployment.
The development of special manpower information continues to be an important aspect of the work of the economics and research branch. In co-operation with the dominion bureau of statistics, a study of multiple jobholding was completed during the year. The report sheds light on the magnitude of multiple jobholding or moonlighting, as it is frequently referred to, its regional concentration, the characteristics of multiple jobholders and their work patterns.
The continuing work of the branch in reviewing local labour market situations in all parts of Canada was helpful in designating the 35 development areas. The Department of Labour has the responsibility of designating areas that might qualify for special federal assistance under the area development program. The economics and research branch at present is engaged in a study which is aimed at evaluating the appropriateness of the present system of selecting areas.
The branch is continuing its studies of the manpower effects of technological change. Consideration is being given to concentrating research on major new technologies in the early stage of use in industry. Particular emphasis will continue to be given to occupational trends studies. In addition to the report published early this year which deals with occupational trends on a national basis, work is now proceeding on the changing occupational structure of specific industries.
May I now say a word on a subject which has been discussed frequently and at some length by hon. members during the current session of this parliament. I have myself referred at some length, during recent statements in the house, to the work of the board of trustees, and it may be that hon. members will wish to raise points that I can deal with later today. Hon. members will recall that the trustees submitted their first report, as required under the legislation passed last October, on March 9, 1904. Since this report was submitted the trustees have taken action with respect to the president of the S.I.U. Mr. H. C. Banks was removed from office and replaced by one of the members of the staff of the board of trustees.

Supply-Labour
The trustees have been able to develop a joint approach in bargaining which is now taking place between the employers representing the companies and each of the individual unions coming under the trusteeship.
The principal accomplishment of the trustees, to date, however, has been the removal of the harassment on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway which has plagued this water highway for many years. It is still too soon, of course, to say that all the problems besetting the maritime unions in Canada have been solved or removed, but I do feel the trustees have made a substantial beginning in this important task. The Department of Labour and other government agencies have endeavoured to co-operate with them fully in carrying out the difficult task they have been asked to undertake.
Hon. members know there has not been an opportunity for the full exercise of democratic rights on the part of many Canadian seamen in their union activities for some years. This was one of the main reasons for establishing the trusteeship, and is one of the basic objectives which the trustees have in mind. The trustees have initiated steps to ensure that proper procedures are developed for the election of officers in the S.I.U., which will be taking place over the next few months.
Steps are also being taken to encourage separate union organizations for officer personnel including engineers and other seamen as recommended in the Norris report. These proposed steps I understand have the support of the unions concerned and of the Canadian Labour Congress. Proposals have been made to reduce initiation and assessment fees in the S.I.U.
These are all important steps which the trustees have taken and which should help them to accomplish the over-all task which parliament has assigned to them. Later this session members of the House of Commons will have an opportunity to meet with the chairman of the board of trustees, and I am sure will be able to secure more detailed information which will be helpful to them in assessing the work of the board of trustees and in restoring democratic practices and democratic attitudes in the seafarers union. It is obvious that the development of democracy, after the kind of regime that has existed in this union for a long period of time, will not be an easy task and will not be undertaken overnight.
Later on today I would like to make a statement on the larger question of automa-
[Mr. MacEachen.l
tion, if this would meet with the approval of the committee, but at this stage I wish to refer briefly to the new manpower consultative service which is also provided for in the first vote of the department. This service was set up this year to assess the implications of industrial change on manpower in industry, and develop measures to alleviate manpower dislocation attributable to technological change. It will administer the program of research incentives for investigations at the plant level into the manpower effects of technological change and will also administer the program of financial assistance for relocation of employees displaced by technological change. The director and three officers have been appointed, after cross-country competition. Two additional officers will be appointed as soon as suitable candidates are found.
The special services branch's main functions relate to the stimulation of winter employment. It is charged at the present time with the administration and the development of the municipal winter works incentive program; the winter house building incentive program; the supplementary federal government winter construction program. This branch also administers the federal-provincial farm labour program.
Some changes were introduced into the municipal winter works incentive program last year which were designed to further increase the program's effectiveness. The maximum federal incentive payment on municipal buildings was increased from $50,000 to $100,000 to encourage the inclusion of larger buildings under the program.
In respect of projects carried out in designated development areas and areas of high winter unemployment, the federal incentive payment was increased from 50 per cent to 60 per cent of direct payroll costs. The period of the program for 1963-64 was reduced from seven and one half months to the six month period November 1 to April 30, so as to concentrate more work in the actual winter months.
During the course of the 1963-64 program 7,320 applications for projects were accepted. These were submitted by 2,755 local authorities, including Indian bands. The total estimated expenditure on projects undertaken in 1963-64 is $282,000,000. The program this year provided an estimated 165,000 men with approximately 6,875,000 man days of work. The figures in 1962-63 were 146,000 men for 6,200,000 man days. The federal government's contribution to direct payroll costs for 1963-64 has been estimated at better than $52 million,

while in the previous year the amount expended was approximately $31 million.
The winter house building incentive program was introduced during the winter of 1963-64 to increase winter employment in the house building industry. It provides, as hon. members know, for the direct payment of a $500 incentive to the first purchaser or owner-builder of a house substantially built during the period December 1, 1963 through March 31, 1964. As evidence of the success of the program, representations were made by the industry for an extension of the inspection date because of shortages which occurred due to the heavy demand on materials and skilled labour. The extension was granted to April 15, 1964.
Under the program 32,647 applications for the incentive payment were received. Of these approximately 3,400 were cancelled and 4,700 were rejected at first or final inspection because they did not meet the conditions of the program. This leaves approximately 24,529 active applications which covered 28,213 dwelling units. The total amount of incentive payments will be approximately $4 million.
This program was successful in creating additional employment for construction workers last winter. The program also created additional employment for workers in the manufacture, transportation and sale of building materials.
As announced in the house on June 23, both the municipal winter works incentive program will be continued next year. It may be possible for me later in the day to tell hon. members of certain changes we are contemplating with a view to increasing the effectiveness of both the municipal winter works program and the winter house building program for next season.
May I report to the committee on the experimental program for the employment of older workers. The older worker employment and training incentive program was initiated by the federal government on an experimental basis last winter. Under its provisions the Department of Labour pays 50 per cent of monthly wages or $75 per month, whichever is less, to employers hiring workers aged 45 and over who met certain conditions for new jobs in insurable employment. Payments are made for a total period not exceeding 12 months. It was recognized that breaking in a new employee, particularly one who had been unemployed for six months or more, could be costly to an employer. Therefore it appeared reasonable to share these
Supply-Labour
costs with an employer until such time as the worker had become fully productive. Twelve months was considered to be an adequate period for this purpose.
The program resulted in some 1,948 older workers obtaining employment, all of whom had been unemployed for at least six of the previous nine months. The program has, in my judgment, been reasonably successful. It has led to the employment of approximately 2,000 older workers, and it will provide the Department of Labour with better insight into the whole problem of the employment of older workers. At the present time the department is continuing an evaluation of this particular program and I hope this evaluation, which we expect to be completed very soon, will allow us to plan future action on behalf of older workers. This obviously was an experimental program, and I hope it will continue to be possible in the department to take the risk of experimenting in providing opportunities for the employment of older Canadians.
May I say a word about federal assistance for technical and vocational training, which is having a substantial impact on the development of a skilled labour force. Since April 1, 1961, when the new technical and vocational training agreements with the provinces came into effect, Federal approval has been given to sharing in provincial expenditures for 572 projects to build and equip new schools and to make additions and alterations and provide equipment for existing schools. The estimated total cost of these projects was $583.4 million; the estimated federal contribution was $352.5 million; the projects will provide 159,417 new student places. Enrolments in all programs have increased. There has been a dramatic increase in the number of vocational high schools; technician training programs have enrolments to capacity, apprenticeship continues to increase, and training classes of unemployed have continued to increase in the face of much improved employment conditions.
Under agreements which provided for sharing at the rate of 75 per cent in capital expenditures incurred by the provinces before April 1, 1963 there was an initial year largely devoted to the planning of new facilities. The following year, 1962-63, was a period of incentive construction. By year's end the accumulated total of federal contributions toward buildings completed and equipment installed had reached $197.5 million. In 196364, as previously approved projects reached

Supply-Labour
completion, the amount of capital assistance claimed by the provinces fell to about $102 million for the year. The December, 1963 amendments to the Technical and Vocation Training Assistance Act extended the period for sharing at the rate of 75 per cent in capital expenditures for most of the provinces, and the planning of additional facilities has been resumed.
In the current planning of training facilities and programs, considerably more attention is being paid to the training of adults. The new legislation provides increased incentives for the development of training programs, in co-operation with industry, for employed workers. These programs will provide the worker with the basic knowledge of mathematics, science and communications necessary for him to enter training for a skilled occupation. It is a fact that one of the obstacles facing certain classes of workers in acquiring needed skills is their lack of a basic knowledge of mathematics and science which would enable them to acquire the skills which would allow them to take on gainful employment. This training program covers industrial apprenticeships and programs for the retraining of employees who without such training would be displaced because of technological or other industrial changes.
Another program for adults which is receiving increased attention is the program for retraining the unemployed. Experience has demonstrated that the most effective way to permanently remove many of these workers from the ranks of the unemployed is to upgrade their basic education to the point where they can proceed to training for occupational skills, either in school classes or in industrial courses while employed. Though the severity of unemployment has lessened, the long run advantages of this type of training warrant the additional expenditures incurred to support it. Certainly the training programs that have been developed, and the capital expenditure program with which the hon. member for Ontario was associated, have had a very marked impact in upgrading the labour force in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, this concludes my remarks in introducing the estimates of my department. I do apologize to the committee for taking up some time in outlining the activities of the Department of Labour. Before I conclude I should like to anticipate a question that might be asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre especially, having to do with the matter of labour standards.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to conclude my remarks by referring to the fact that this is a very appropriate occasion on which to discuss the estimates of the Department of Labour, because on Monday next all Canada will pause to pay tribute to the great contribution that the labouring people of Canada have made to the development of this country, and to the great role that organized labour has played in the development of ever increasing participation by the working people of Canada in the wealth and welfare of our country.

Mr. Chairman, in his opening remarks the Minister of Labour mentioned the fact that we have already devoted one day to the estimates of the Department of Labour, and he is quite right; one day was devoted to this subject when we discussed interim supply. However, one day may not be sufficient, in view of past experience with the estimates of this department and the fact that the Department of Labour has played

such an important part in the economy of our country in recent years. Bearing in mind previous discussions of the estimates of this department, many more days have been taken up in dealing with these estimates than perhaps those of any other department which have been brought before the committee for their approval.
It seems rather strange, Mr. Chairman, that this appears to be a new approach by this government, namely that ministers warn the House of Commons and its members that they are prepared to bring in legislation provided the promise is made that there will be no debate or that there will be debate for only one or two days. This is a condition that always seems to be placed on any needed legislation being put before the house. Then, of course, the Minister of Labour, in a mild way, reminded us of the fact that we had already spent one day on the estimates of his department when we considered interim supply. In view of the fact that we have spent only one day dealing with this matter, I believe some hon. members will wish to express their opinions with respect to the many matters that are involved in these estimates, but I hope we may be able to pass them during today's discussion.
The Minister of Labour has repeated statements he has made on previous occasions, and has pointed out with some satisfaction that employment is up, unemployment is down and there is a marked improvement in this respect. I remember very well that beginning with the year 1961 that condition began to show itself, namely that employment was rising and unemployment was showing a marked decline. When I pointed this out with some satisfaction on a number of occasions in the House of Commons, those who now claim there is a marked improvement in this connection were very critical and spent many hours pointing up the fact that unemployment was a very serious problem. Of course it still is, Mr. Chairman; because how can anyone say with a straight face that there is a marked improvement in the employment situation in this country when there were only 28,000 fewer unemployed in July of this year than there were last year?
However, as I pointed out during the discussion on interim supply, this points up a very important aspect of the employment picture in this country, in that not sufficient jobs are being created to take care of the teen agers who are entering the labour force; because in this respect the figures show an increase-I might say a marked increase, to use the same words as the minister-over
Supply-Labour
the same period last year. The Minister of Labour has not treated this as a serious matter, nor has he told us what is being done to create jobs for these teen agers who are entering our labour market.
The minister made reference to what he termed the special programs this government has introduced to deal with seasonal unemployment. Are they new programs he is talking about, Mr. Chairman? I ask this question because at the moment I can think of only one program that has met with success, and that is the winter-built homes program. Even here it remains to be seen whether success will be achieved this coming winter in the same way that the programs introduced by the previous administration in 1958, 1959 and 1961 met with success.
The other program mentioned by the Minister of Labour was the employment of older workers. It seems to me that if a program is not successful it is termed experimental. There seems to be a tendency to make statements that sound as though something is actually being done. I take as an example the Postmaster General's statement in a press release today. He said it is his intention, in co-operation with the Minister of Public Works, to help the winter unemployment situation by building a number of small post office buildings throughout Canada in designated areas. This is a program that was started back in the time this party was in office, and it met with a great deal of success. However, Mr. Chairman, an excuse is being offered in this release by saying that many of those buildings under the Post Office Department were not proceeded with because of site problems, cost and staff limitations. We also had the announcement today that some 185 locations were involved in the post office building program, subject to satisfactory arrangements being made with respect to the acquisition of suitable sites and to obtaining tenders reasonable in cost.
All this is very fine, but I would ask, in view of the failure during the past year to undertake any part of this program, whether this is only a fine sounding statement which is being put out, or will any actual developments take place as a result of the announcement. We must take things as they are presented to us and hope that some steps will be taken.
Mention has been made of the municipal winter works program, in which I realize the Minister of Labour takes great pride, as well he should. The municipal winter works program was not looked upon, when it was

Supply-Labour
first introduced in 1958-59, as something which would be of a permanent character. As a matter of fact it was looked upon as something that would fail, as a puny effort. Yet it has been a successful program in that year after year there has been a marked increase in activity and a greater participation in the program on the part of the municipalities. It is a program that is here for many years to come.
We should like to know, with regard to the experimental program for the employment of older workers, what was the total cost of this experiment. I am not critical of this program in this respect, because we are all interested in the welfare of the older workers; certainly I have been interested in them in the past. I should like to know whether the cost is so great that the experiment is not worth while. I realize that the policing of the program must be a terrible headache, and whether it can be carried out successfully in view of the stringent regulations which are applied to it is something the Minister of Labour should tell us today during the discussion of his estimates.
The minister did not touch upon a number of matters about which I think we are entitled to know, particularly matters on which action has continually been promised. We would like to know what is the state of the unemployment insurance fund and whether this fund will be sufficiently strong to carry itself in the coming winter months, or whether more loans have to be made to bolster it. What has happened to the report of the Gill commission on which the government has been sitting for over a year and a half? The only action which has been taken is the announcement that the national employment service will be transferred to the jurisdiction of the labour department; and I understand that change is now in the process of being brought about. But what has happened to the rest of the report of the Gill commission? It is a report on which the present government said they would act immediately on assuming office. Where is the labour code? The Minister says he will have a resolution on the order paper before the calendar changes to October. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre queried that and wanted to know in what year. Time has dragged on and no action has been taken in this regard.
What about the promised legislation on hours of work? What about the promised legislation on minimum wages? What has been done about these matters? Nothing has

been done to our knowledge. Certainly nothing has appeared on the order paper to show that the government wish to carry out the promises they have made. What about this most important subject now being discussed and which has been discussed for a number of years-a matter which has been looked at with some apprehension by those who may be affected-automation and technological change? We endeavoured to do something about it through the introduction of a bill in the House of Commons. We planned to call a conference between industry and labour to work out regulations and details respecting such a co-operative plan with the provinces. Today we hear that all that is being done is some research and study on the subject. Although that may be necessary, I venture the guess. that research and study of this problem has been carried to the point where some action could now be taken by the department to see whether an alleviation of this problem could be brought about.
We made a start on labour-management cooperation with the setting up of the productivity council, and I think one of its most important achievements was in being able to bring about better understanding between management and labour for the first time in the history of this country. But with the elimination of the productivity council by the government nothing further has been heard about labour-management co-operation. The meetings which used to be held under the jurisdiction of the productivity council now seem to have been discontinued altogether, and we hear no more about the worth-while effort which was made at that time.
As far as the trusteeship on the great lakes is concerned I might say that no one- at least not I-has any intention of trying to upset or interfere in the affairs of those who work on the great lakes, because I think it is necessary to bring about some peace on the great lakes in order not to jeopardize our economy. However, I am not satisfied with the manner in which trustees have proceeded, and I am far from satisfied that they have brought about a solution, in the long run, to the problems on the great lakes. It seems to me that the trustees, who were appointed as a result of the recommendations made in the Norris report, have ignored the report completely. As a matter of fact, on reading the summary of the whole situation we find that Mr. Millard never even read the Norris report; he felt he could proceed on his own.

In my opinion the trusteeship was set up because of the Norris report; indeed, one of its main recommendations was the setting up of the trusteeship. It seems to me as though the trustees are trying during their term of office to create an atmosphere on the great lakes in which there will be no disturbance of Canadian ships in United States ports. That seems to me to be their main objective. And that they have done, by whatever methods they have used to arrive at an agreement with Mr. Paul Hall, the head of the S.I.U. in the United States. It seems obvious to me that some satisfactory arrangement was made to him, because we have had no harassment of Canadian ships in United States ports during this present season.
What is going to happen when the trustees, who seem to be anxious to get rid of the undertaking that parliament gave them, move out of the picture? Is the whole situation going to revert to what it was originally? I cannot see how the problem has been solved by the trustees in any way so far as the days ahead are concerned. We read that a democratic vote is to be held, but we also read with some apprehension that those who would oppose the present incumbent in office are being shifted around to get them out of the way so they cannot participate. The trustees only act when public opinion brings these matters to their attention. Then they endeavour to rectify the situation and do so, but some doubt is left in my mind with regard to whether the trustees are really on the job and actually know what is happening.
It is fine for the trustees to say that many of the people who were associated with the former president have now atoned for their sins, have gone through purgatory and are prepared to lead a new life.
They have gone through a whitewash.

That is all to their credit, but certainly their actions with regard to the holding of a democratic vote on the great lakes would lead me to believe they have not spent enough time in purgatory. I am worried that the trustees are too anxious to finish the job and leave the situation in the same position it was when they came into the picture. I see no reason why this will not be so, because I can see no great changes in the situation. There has been a temporary lull only, and when the trustees move out I think the situation will revert to what it was previously.

With Labour day coming on Monday, when all of us pay tribute to those who have left their mark on the Canadian labour movement, I wish to add my words to those of the Minister of Labour and say how much we appreciate those men and women in the labour force who have dedicated their lives and energy to the betterment of conditions for those people engaged in the building of our country, those engaged in the labour movement and the protection of our democratic way of life.
It is with a great deal of regret that I refer to the passing of William Jenoves who was called "Mr. Labour" in the Toronto area and who played such a tremendous part in the labour movement in Canada. He passed away recently, and I understand his funeral will be held in Toronto on Tuesday. It is men such as Billy Jenoves who have worked unselfishly in the interests of the men and women of our labour force in years gone by and who have laid a firm foundation and created a truly good reputation for the labour people of this country. To such men we are thankful, because it is through their participation and co-operation that we are now able to enjoy the Canada that we have today.

Mr. Chairman, it would be easy for me to make a speech of the labour estimates simply by referring to last year's Hansard and looking at the speeches which members made then, because really nothing of any importance has been accomplished since the minister made his introductory remarks last year and members commented upon them in discussing the labour estimates.
It was good to hear the minister say today in his concluding remarks that he expected to bring in a resolution or bill dealing with a national labour code before the end of the month. It is good to hear this, but we in this group have been hearing such statements by other Liberal cabinet ministers ever since Mackenzie King made such a statement in a speech in 1919. It is probably just as well that the hon. member for Hamilton East is not here at the moment, in that I expect he would be on his feet interrupting me as he interrupted the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre last year, because he would construe my approach as a partisan one.
In recent years members of various parties including our own have presented private members' bills calling for the provision of fair wages, a maximum work week and holidays with pay. When the Liberal party were in opposition they supported us, of course, but now they say we do not need such

Supply-Labour
legislation because the government is going to introduce a national labour code which will provide for all these things. I was glad to hear the minister say that it would at least be on the order paper before the end of the month. When the government will proceed with it is, of course, a very good question. I hope the minister will not be too surprised if I say I am from Missouri and am even a little sceptical about his promise it will be on the order paper this month.
So far as fair wages are concerned, I hope the code will provide a minimum of $1.25 an hour for all federal employees. In case the minister and other members of the house do not know it, I direct their attention to the fact that there are people working for the federal government who still do not receive that much an hour. The charwomen who clean the offices in this building are prevailing rate employees, and they are paid the munificient sum of 95 cents an hour. I wish the minister would not only bring in the new code but would also use his influence on his colleague, the President of the Privy Council, who apparently is in charge of this matter, to get him to undo the zipper on his heart and take some action for the benefit of these people. It is long overdue.
Surely it is also time something was done about establishing a maximum work week. Surely we do not have to wait for the new labour code to be introduced. The same applies to the provision of holidays with pay. Certainly we need a national labour code which will provide that everyone is entitled to holidays with pay after working for the greater part of the year, but do we need that kind of law before the government lives up to the spirit contained in such a law? Surely it is time every person working for the federal government should be protected in this way.
This includes the secretaries who work for members of parliament. They are human beings like everybody else, and are entitled to the same rights as everybody else. Since they have now been working for well over a year without holidays, surely they are entitled to holidays with pay now. I hope the rumours we have heard that treasury board has turned this down are false. If they are true, I hope treasury board will reconsider its recommendation and come forward with a favourable decision very quickly. I am sorry; I am wrong. It is the internal economy commission, and I hope they will reconsider this matter and come

in with a favourable recommendation very quickly.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that the matter of collective bargaining for government employees does not come directly or exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour. However, I want to say that personally I am very disappointed that the Liberal party, having announced several years ago that it favoured the extension of collective bargaining to federal employees, has failed to implement that promise. I recognize some of the difficulties in implementing this kind of principle. I recognize that the organizations which represent the employees overlap, and that there are large problems of detail in implementing this promise. It would seem to me, however, that the difficulties could have been and should have been overcome by now. I hope it will not be too long before the promise made by the Liberal party that federal government employees would have the right to bargain collectively with regard to wages, salaries and working conditions, will be implemented.
If this promise had been implemented, as I think it should have been by now, we would not be faced with the present hassle with regard to the salary increases recently granted to group B employees. Here we have
65.000	employees working for the government and I am told that 10,000 of those, even after the latest increases have been approved, will still make less than $3,000 annually after they reach the maximum of the salary classification to which they belong. If you take into account all those who have not reached their maximum the figure of
10.000	would probably be doubled. This means that we have clerks, typists, office equipment operators, messengers and clerical assistants who are still making less than $60 per week. I wonder how those of us who are interested in the welfare of the ordinary citizen can believe these people are able to live on any decent standard. It seems to me obvious that something ought to be done now.
I do not know whether the rumours are true to the effect that the civil service commission recommended a substantially greater increase than the government finally approved. Nor do I know whether it is true that the President of the Privy Council was one of those who opposed the increase which the civil service commission recommended. I do know that if the government had implemented its promise that civil servants would have the right to bargain collec-

tively, this kind of difficulty which we are now facing would have been overcome; because it would have been settled in the normal and proper way in which all employee problems should be settled, that is by collective bargaining.
I should like to say something very briefly Mr. Chairman, about the comments of the minister with regard to the unemployment situation, with regard to the programs which the federal government implemented for retraining and to deal with such problems as automation. I am not at all satisfied that we have licked the problem of unemployment. It is standard procedure for the old parties, when they are in opposition, to say that the rate of unemployment is too high; but when those parties become the government they say the situation is much better, that the number of unemployed is less than it was. Of course the number of unemployed is less than it was this time last year. However, the rate is still one which is of great concern, and it should be of great concern to all of us The rate at which unemployment is dropping has decreased very sharply in each month recently.
I should like to point out to the members of this committee that as respected and as conservative an economist as Dr. Firestone has predicted that unemployment will increase rather sharply in the next couple of years. I have heard nothing from the minister or from any other government spokesman which would indicate the government really has any plans for dealing with this basic problem. I think to a large extent the reduction in unemployment is an accident for which this government should not take any credit. The minister shakes his head. This is my opinion, and I feel that if we have a chance to discuss the problem in detail we can demonstrate this very clearly.
The minister referred in some detail to the programs the government has introduced to take care of retraining. Certainly we are doing more than we have done in other years, but I suggest to the minister and the government that the programs really only go a small way toward meeting the problem. It is not my intention to deal with this aspect in any detail today, but there have been some very disquieting reports in newspapers like the Toronto Star, which is not noted for its hostility to this government. These reports have referred to the large number of people who begin the training program but who drop out before their training period has been completed. They drop out because the amount
Supply-Labour
of money they are given to help them maintain themselves and their families while they are taking this training is woefully inadequate. I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to arranging for the industrial relations committee to meet so we could discuss in detail these training programs which the government has begun or is planning. We could also hear representatives from the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and other organizations interested in labour problems.
I want to deal with a question which has concerned this house for the last couple of years, Mr. Chairman, and with which the minister dealt very briefly today. I refer to the situation on the great lakes. I want to try to do this is a non-partisan way. What I say will to some extent be my own personal opinion. It is no secret that there were and are differences of opinion in all parties about what happened in the past on the great lakes, about what was done when we passed the legislation establishing the board of trustees, and about how well the trustees have succeeded in accomplishing the job entrusted to them.
I begin by saying I view with a great deal of scepticism the criticisms, comments and questions which have been raised on this issue by members of the official opposition. Listening to them one would think all the fault lies with the government, but the fact is that Mr. Banks was head of the S.I.U. of Canada for a long period of time, including the six years during which the present official opposition was the government. That government was acquainted with some of the things Mr. Banks was doing.
I remind members of the committee that on one occasion the president of one of the large shipping companies wrote to an official of the Department of Labour, Mr. Wilson, enclosing a copy of a letter from Mr. Banks in which he asked the company to ignore the provisions of Canadian labour legislation, to ignore decisions of the Canada labour relations board, and to recognize certain members of the S.I.U. as being entitled to employment even though the Canadian labour relations board had ruled these people were covered by an agreement with another union. In his letter Mr. Banks promised to indemnify the shipping company if it were sued for damages.
That was an obvious breach of the Canada Labour Relations Act but the former minister of labour, who is now sitting on the opposition benches, did nothing about it. When the

Supply-Labour
opposition talks about Mr. Banks it must accept part of the responsibility for not having taken any action while it was in power. I have noted members of the opposition patting themselves on the back because they appointed Mr. Justice Norris to inquire into the situation, but the fact is that they did not establish the Norris commission until the Canadian Labour Congress and the unions affiliated with it tied up the St. Lawrence seaway.
In discussing this matter of the great lakes I wish to say I was amazed and shocked that a member of the House of Commons, in the year 1964, would make the kind of speech which was made by the hon. member for Athabasca in the house on July 25 last. I wish to quote a couple of lines from his speech on that occasion, and members can find his words recorded on Hansard at pages 6044 to 6048. This is one of the things he said:
"I do not believe we need labour unions at all, if we do our job in this House of Commons."
There is not a democratic country in the world which does not have labour unions, which is not proud of the labour unions it has, and which does not encourage their growth; but I have not heard a single member of the hon. member's party repudiate his statement. Further on he said:
This is still a jungle and the labour bosses are
the biggest apes in the jungle__We should put
these labour bosses with criminal records out of business for five years at least.
There have been very few labour officials, let alone labour leaders, convicted of any crime in this country. Further on the hon. member enumerated some of the things of which he accused labour leaders of being guilty:
-sedition, violence upon the person, organized murder, conspiracy to maim-
I am sure hon. members in all parties who are interested in labour will agree with me when I reject completely the allegation that labour leaders in this country have been guilty of these kinds of crimes. The hon. member ought to list the number of labour leaders who have been convicted or even charged with such crimes. I say this is false and has no truth at all in it. I also say I am surprised that the former minister of labour in the Conservative government did not make mention of this when he talked about Labour day and the importance of labour.
Returning to the question of the S.I.U., I am one who voted for the legislation which established the board of trustees for the

maritime unions. I recognized then, and I recognize now, that the trustees would not have an easy job. After all, the United States government has indicated its support for as few changes as possible. The United States labour movement has supported Mr. Paul Hall and the S.I.U. of North America.
During the years Mr. Banks was in power the Canadian shipping companies, especially Canada Steamship Lines, were happy to go along with Mr. Banks to the mutual advantage of both. I recognized the fact that the legislation was a new departure and that the job of the trustees would not be easy. I was quite happy with the members who were appointed to the board. I had great respect for the contribution which Mr. Millard had made to the labour movement. I knew of Judge Lippe's activities as a successful arbiter of labour disputes, and we had heard good things about Mr. Justice Dryer.
I have not discussed this with other members of my party or members of other parties; I speak for myself alone, and I must say that I am disappointed with the progress which has been made. It is true that harassment of Canadian ships in United States ports has stopped, but I wonder how much credit the trustees can take for that. After all, there was no harassment of Canadian ships so long as Mr. Banks was in power. Harassment of Canadian ships did not start until steps were taken by the Canadian labour movement and by the government, through this legislation, to clip the wings of Mr. Banks. If all we wanted to do was stop the harassment of Canadian ships we would not have got involved in the legislation; therefore I do not give the trustees very much credit for this situation.
What else have the trustees done? Well, Mr. Banks is out. I do not know why they finally removed him from the presidency of the S.I.U. Stories in Canadian newspapers which continued until a day or two before he was removed indicated that on the whole the trustees were not unhappy with him. I do not know whether the fact that Mr. Banks apparently arranged for the tapping of the telephones of the trustees was responsible for the decision.
The point I wish to make is this. The officials who worked with Mr. Banks, the officials who were part of the conspiracy in the gangster empire he built up, are still in power. A good public relations job has been done-I do not want now to discuss who has done it-to try to convince the Canadian people that the S.I.U. was not so bad, that

Mr. Justice Norris was prejudiced, that he had exaggerated, and so on. I do not wish to repeat what Mr. Justice Norris said about Mr. McLaughlin, Mr. Heinekey and Mr. Swait, because members of this committee who are interested will have read the Norris report. I wish to quote just a couple of paragraphs from the Globe and Mail of May 2, 1964 under the heading "Court found It Impossible to Believe Testimony of Banks". This is a summary of the judgment by Judge Wagner, now attorney general of the province of Quebec, the judge who sentenced Mr. Banks to five years in prison. I want to read a couple of paragraphs to make clear what Judge Wagner had to say about Mr. McLaughlin.
Leonard (Red) McLaughlin, SIU vice president and heir apparent to the union presidency under the federal trusteeship-Judge Wagner described him as Banks' trusted adviser and the man who endeavoured to come to Bank's rescue during the trial. He referred to Richard Greaves' evidence that McLaughlin in August, 1957, "has appeared with the daily report referring to the doings of Capt. Walsh" and said this was the signal of an explosion.
"The court wishes to state that it entertains very little regard for the conduct in this respect of Mr. McLaughlin who more than any other member of the union was familiar with the sentiments of the man at the top," the Judge said.
"This Mr. McLaughlin in his testimony before the court gave us the definite impression that he was bent on favouring the accused by attempting to minimize the motives which had prompted the beating of Capt. Walsh."
I could go on, but I think this indicates clearly that Judge Wagner at least shared the sentiments of Mr. Justice Norris with regard to Mr. McLaughlin. Yet the trustees have obviously decided that despite the voluminous testimony relating to Mr. McLaughlin and other top officials of the S.I.U. of Canada they should be permitted-indeed, I would go further and say that in my opinion they are being encouraged-to continue as leaders of the union. Speaking for myself-and I wish to make it clear I am speaking only for myself-may I say that if the total accomplishment by the passage of the legislation establishing the board of trustees will be the removal of Mr. Banks as president of the S.I.U.; if this is to be the total accomplishment which we shall see from the trustees, then I for one shall be sorry I voted for the legislation setting up this board.
I know the trustees have been faced with a difficult task. It may be that I am wrong. It may be they have done a great deal more than we know about. I hope the minister can prevail on the trustees to come to Ottawa and appear before the industrial relations
Supply-Labour
committee, not next November or December or in January of 1965, but now. They should appear now, because if they are doing a job as claimed this is the place where they can tell us what they are doing.
I wish to mention some of the questions I should like-
