Just five minutes. I should like to know from the trustees why union elections are being held now. I have carefully examined the constitution of the S.I.U. of Canada, and I suggest the Minister of Labour should do the same. I read it in the presence of one of the most eminent labour lawyers in Canada.
Mr. Lewis?

Not Mr. Lewis. As I read the constitution, the election should not have been held until 1965. I suggest to the Minister of Labour and to the trustees that if they wish to develop the democratic forces of the S.I.U. the constitutional provisions calling for elections in 1965 should have been adhered to, so there might have been another year for the rank and file democratic, clean forces to develop and organize. It seems to me that what you have now is an election as between two slates of officers each intimately connected with the Banks machine.
I should like to know why the do not ship list is in fact still being enforced at the present time, despite all the protestations of the trustees that the list was destroyed and no longer exists. A number of people have applied for readmission to the S.I.U., people who were placed on the do not ship list. They applied to the board of trustees, and my information is that they were referred to Commodore Robertson who heads the appeal committee set up by Mr. Banks and continued by the trustees.
A number of people, 25 or more, have applied for readmission. In the last issue of the Canadian Sailor published by the S.I.U. under the supervision of the board of trustees there appears a report by Commodore Robertson on his work. He lists the people who have applied for readmission and the disposition of their cases. One of those who applied for readmission was a Mr. Carmel

Supply-Labour
Deguire. Mr. Deguire was turned down by Commodore Robertson on the ground that he could not prove his membership in the S.I.U. and that the S.I.U. of Canada has no record of his membership. Mr. Chairman, Mr. De-guire's name appeared on a do not ship list which was filed with the Norris commission as exhibit 0-269 and attested to by Mr. Banks on the witness stand as being a correct extract from the do not ship list.
Similarly, Mr. Chairman, a Mr. Ken Lewis was turned down on the ground that there was no record that he had been a member of the S.I.U. Mr. Lewis' name also appears on the do not ship list in exhibit 0-269. The transcript of the evidence which Mr. Justice Norris heard and all the material which was filed with Mr. Justice Norris is under the supervision and control of Mr. Justice Dryer and the trustees. Aren't they interested? Don't they care? Aren't they going to take the trouble to look at what those exhibits show?
Here is another man, Mr. Donald Swan. He appealed to Commodore Robertson for readmission to the S.I.U. Commodore Robertson turned him down, and I quote from his report which is published in The Canadian Sailor, which says that the applicant was unable to produce evidence of membership and, further, that the S.I.U. could not trace membership.
If the Minister of Labour will take the trouble to look at the report of Mr. Justice Norris, the second part entitled "Schedule", at page 569, in a section of about 20 pages which lists people whose names appeared on the do not ship list, he will find the name of Donald Swan. How much more, I ask, do the board of trustees need?
Then there is David Bath, who applied for readmission and was turned down on the same ground by Commodore Robertson. His name appears at page 537 of the Norris report. Here is a really difficult one. A Mr. Henry Ranta appealed for readmission to the S.I.U. and was turned down on the ground that the applicant was unable to produce evidence of membership in the S.I.U. Well, Mr. Chairman, his name appears on page 564 of the Norris report. It may be that Commodore Robertson and the trustees have difficulty in this instance because instead of his name being spelled "Ranta" it is spelled "Ranto". I realize there is a tremendous difference between "Ranta" and "Ranto" and intelligent people who read might have difficulty in making that connection.
I do not wish to take up the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman; I think I have

indicated enough to show that there is a great deal which the trustees need to look at and which in my opinion and in the opinion of many others they have not yet looked at.
I wish to close by referring to just one other case. This concerns a Mr. John Wood, a former official-I think a vice president-of the S.I.U. of Canada. He was expelled-he was not on the do not ship list-after one of the kangaroo court trials which the S.I.U. was so prone to hold under Mr. Banks. Mr. John Wood tried to get back to work. After all, like the rest of us, he has to eat. After he failed in various other ways he wrote to the president pro tern, Mr. Charles Turner, asking for permission to go back to work. Mr. Turner wrote a letter to Mr. Wood, and in this connection I might say I am personally ashamed that any official of a trade union would write such a letter. The Minister of Labour knows about this letter because I sent him a copy. He said to Mr. Wood, in effect, "Yes, we will let you go back to work under certain conditions".
What were those conditions, Mr. Chairman? I wish to just read a couple of them. One was that Mr. Wood would tender to the union, in a form suitable to S.I.U. counsel, an agreement not to participate in union affairs, and another was that he would not engage in activities hostile or harmful to the status of the union and its international in any areas of union interest. In other words "You can come back to work if you keep your mouth shut and never do anything to disturb the status quo; never say anything that will get members of the S.I.U. to vote for somebody other than Mr. McLaughlin" and the rest of the thugs who are still in control of the S.I.U.
I wrote a letter to Mr. Justice Dryer asking him if this was not a violation of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I had no answer except an acknowledgment. There may be a legal question as to whether this action comes within the provisions of that act. But, Mr. Chairman, how can any reasonable person, how can the board of trustees justify this action in any way on the basis of equity or justice?
I hope the board of trustees will appear before the industrial relations committee next week and give us information which will indicate that the things I have said and which other members have said are wrong. I want to say now that if they do; if they can show they have done the work which was entrusted to them in accordance with the pro-

visions of the act, and have done the things which I think they have not done, I will be the first to commend them and to apologize for making the kind of speech I have made today. However, I say that until they do that -and the sooner they do it the better, and I would again urge on the Minister of Labour that he appeal to them to come before the industrial relations committee quickly-I for one am, to say the least, disappointed with the job they have done. I do not believe they have moved quickly enough or that they have dealt with the basic problems that were with us when we discussed the legislation which the minister proposed and voted for the establishment of the board of maritime trustees.

Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Labour are rather interesting, because they enable us to deal with extremely sensitive points of our economy, especially with one which is now giving rise to most of the problems and requires most of our attention, unemployment.
When the minister introduced his estimates, he pointed out the progress made during the past year in that particular field.
Of course, we can only be delighted with him at the progress generally accomplished by our economy and as a result of which unemployment has been considerably reduced throughout the country.
However, Mr. Chairman, we must recognize that even though the situation has improved in certain parts of the country, it remains that in the province of Quebec and in the maritime provinces, unemployment is still a nightmare. Indeed, hundreds of thousands of workers are unemployed and have to rely only on unemployment insurance and social assistance benefits to provide for their needs.
For a few years, we have noticed on many occasions that in certain areas, unemployment seems to be a more serious problem than elsewhere in the country.
Last year, when the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), together with the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), decided to designate in our country areas which would receive special attention from the government, we witnessed the recognition by the government of a regional problem. In fact, the government recognized implicitly that our unemployment was regional in character and that the solutions which had to be applied had to be based on the fact that it was a regional situation. Solutions could no longer be applied from
Supply-Labour
coast to coast. A solution taking into account regional characteristics was needed.
Of course, when those areas were designated, like several others 1 was a little disappointed to see the yardstick which had been followed to designate them.
We therefore have made representations to the effect that other criteria be used when the list of those designated areas is revised.
I hope that the Minister of Labour, in cooperation with the Minister of Industry, will be able to say, when a decision is announced in this regard, that he has taken into account the representations and remarks we have made, and I hope the decision will be to everyone's satisfaction.
However, we must admit that the designation of those areas has not solved the problem entirely. Even if the Minister of Industry did state that in 23 out of 35 areas, new industries had been established, we are nevertheless deploring the fact that it has been many years now since a new industry has settled in the Saguenay area. I can only draw the attention of the minister on this very special situation in my area.
I believe that the activities of the area development agency, which I admit, is under the Department of Industry, but in which the Minister of Labour is surely interested, should be enlarged. It should be given more definite work to do because, in my opinion, this area development agency offers real possibilities for bringing solutions to the problems.
At this time, I should like to strongly urge the Minister of Labour to put pressure on his colleague the Minister of Industry, and stress the point with him so that this agency might be given more latitude and a very definite policy, in short a certain authority in that field which apparently is going to be given to it.
A while ago, the minister mentioned the large technical training program, the vocational training schools, as they are called. That program was introduced in 1960 and 1961 by the previous government.
Of course, we must be all satisfied with that favourable development. But I sometimes wonder whether we really consider the problem as a whole, since as late as last week, I had an opportunity to read the report of an American sociologist who had carried a detailed investigation on the future implications of general automation and mechanization in industry.
That same sociologist claims that in the next 50 years, workers will have to change trade or profession at least four times. I

Supply-Labour
think that is a phenomenon which will certainly cause a great upheaval in the general labour situation and in the economy, and which will create tremendous social problems.
It will not be easy for a man who worked in a precise field for ten years and who made all the necessary sacrifices in order to get the technical know-how required in his trade, to qualify in a new field, since the work for which he had qualifications no longer exists.
I feel that if we contemplate the development of manpower in this light, we will have to prepare today the education of future workers, and to prepare it at school, in order to give them a sufficient basis to enable them to acquire very quickly the varied knowledge they will need to cope with the economic development of their future work.
Of course, all that illustrates the need for labour in order to achieve production.
I cannot help thinking of some of the ideas advocated by Social Credit supporters on this question of labour requirement versus production. I must say that, in time, it will be proved that this first idea was good and justified. I think that some of the solutions which have been advocated will have to be applied.
We produce for consumption. Man does not work merely for the pleasure of working; he works in order to obtain the things he needs. If, in future, automation allows us to produce without resorting to labour, I think that we will have to reconsider all our economic, financial, monetary and social philosophy, which will have to undergo far reaching changes.
I would now like, Mr. Chairman, to refer to the winter works program. The minister mentioned earlier today the thousands of man days made possible by this program. Obviously, when I refer to the discussions which took place in 1957 and 1958, when the project was launched by the former government, I can only laugh to myself when recalling the objections from the Liberal benches with regard to that project, when they were still in the opposition. And now that they are in office, they seem to find this formula a successful one, which makes me smile. When in opposition, people have not the same ideas than when they sit on the treasury benches with regard to the same legislative program.
That concept was a happy one under the circumstances, but considering that the great majority of Canadians want to be sincere in this field, it remains that this is only a porary measure, a poultice, so to speak, and that, in the end, the unemployment problem
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John) .1
has not been solved. Indeed, I believe that this formula to encourage winter employment should be entirely reconsidered, because it has become a permanent measure.
If this program designed to alleviate winter unemployment is to be made a permanent fixture, I think it should be established in such a way as to be applicable only to works considered useful, since fantastic amounts are paid to carry them out. In my opinion, it would be logical that this program be reconsidered so that instead of being a winter works program only, it will be a program of year-round municipal works, so that the country and its people can draw the maximum benefits possible, considering the sums invested.
We must all recognize the geographical situation of our country.
The climate in which we live, the millions of dollars we spend during December, January and February to carry out certain municipal works, must be considered. Since these are all municipal works requiring social capital, I believe that 50 per cent of this money is at present being spent unwisely. Moreover, the municipalities cannot do otherwise because of the public pressure they have to bear. In my opinion, the government has given up one of its greatest responsibilities, shifting it upon public managers, our small municipalities. It merely said to the municipalities: You will solve the unemployment problem.
Of course, the municipalities can contribute, but I believe that at this time the full responsibility is put on their shoulders in that field, We put them in a kind of strait-jacket, in the sense that they must complete such works during the period provided for winter works. We make their task doubly difficult, on top of the fact that they are unable to carry out works they feel necessarily useful, sound and suitable. Unfortunately, they are compelled by public opinion, due to pressures brought to bear by citizens, to undertake works that are not always justified.
I believe that, at present, our municipalities are piling up debts while we are squandering public funds by carrying out projects which do not serve, in any way, the general interest of the country.
I suggest that Canada, if it wishes to achieve a reasonable economic status, cannot-in view of its population, its economic position and the burden of its present debt-afford to invest one single dollar of its future credit in an uneconomic project. This is implying a lot, as I believe we are obviously making an

uneconomic investment, and we have practically had to make it for five years. I would even say that, for more than five years, we have invested hundreds of millions in uneconomic municipal works.
I maintain that Canada cannot afford this luxury any more.
We must use all our past, present and future savings, as well as all our credit, for investments in productive fields. We must produce.
Services are not the most desirable thing, at the present time, in the country. We certainly need services, but what we need most, is to develop the field of production, and unless we make such change in our philosophy, we shall continue to face the same economic problem, for that problem is linked with unemployment. The present rate of unemployment may well decrease in a given year, but it will inevitably rise acutely subsequently. An economist forecast recently a forthcoming and quite marked increase in unemployment in this country. This is very encouraging.
I wonder whether we are not in the process of hiding our heads in the sand by encouraging the winter works program in fields which do not create any jobs or production, in fields where investments cannot be recovered.
In saying this, I am thinking of something in particular. In carrying out works under the winter works legislation, productive municipal investments in such fields should be authorized. Obviously the government is unable to create jobs everywhere, to build plants in all sections of the country to create production, but if the government allowed municipalities, within the framework of the winter works formula, to build plants or buildings that could be sublet to small organizations able to undertake some production, I believe this would be a step forward. There are many people with imaginative ideas, who could undertake the production of some articles we presently import; unfortunately, they cannot afford to tie down large sums in a building at the present time. If such a formula were adopted, and if municipalities were allowed to erect buildings they could sublet at so much per square foot to such organizations, I believe that part of our investments could be recovered. We could thus hope to offset the steady increase in our imports.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would like, within the framework of the winter works program, to make a remark on another small problem our municipalities are facing.
Supply-Labour
This small problem, in the end, becomes a major one. When our municipalities undertake winter works, they start by borrowing. Why? In order to finance those works until both federal and provincial subsidies are paid. Since the works start in November and are completed in April, municipalities have to bear this rather heavy burden for six months. I am told that the federal and provincial governments have not yet paid all the money to municipalities for works completed last year. As a result, municipalities must finance the entire cost of winter works for a whole year, and in the long run, after six or seven years, this burden is beginning to be heavily felt in the budgets of our municipalities and to such an extent that I think the saturation point has been reached. Our municipalities will soon be unable to continue to operate under the winter works program.
Last year, Quebec had a remarkable year, but I think that next year there will be a tremendous reduction. Such a reduction or a decrease would neither reflect a lack of needs nor full employment, but the impossibility for administrators to find the necessary financial means for those projects. The only solution would be an increase of municipal taxes which are already excessively high. It is generally known in Quebec as in other provinces that municipal and federal taxes have considerably increased. We are bound to draw the following conclusion: If municipal and school taxes had to be boosted, it was in direct proportion to the increase in municipal expenses under the winter works program. That formula was good up to a certain point but it was only a temporary solution, and I think its best years are over. I feel it will have to be replaced by a more adequate formula. Otherwise, Mr. Chairman, we will find ourselves in the same situation as in 1957-58 when we had three quarters of a million unemployed, if not more, in Canada.
I should like to deal with another point, the $500 bonus for wintertime house construction. The minister seemed quite happy with the apparent results. I say "apparent" because I cannot do otherwise than think that the houses built in winter will reduce summer construction. That is self-evident. Therefore, it means that in the course of a whole year there will not be one house built in excess of those which would have normally been built. I wonder on what evidence the minister has based his statement that the $500 winter house construction incentive has increased the number of houses built.

Supply-Labour
I think the increase is entirely due to normal growth and had nothing to do with this $500 incentive; the only reason is that there was a need for so many family units. Unless you want to build houses which will remain unoccupied, there is no logical reason to state that that grant contributed to the increase in the number of houses built. Statistics will show that the number of family units built in a year will decrease within a certain period of time.
Now, still about the bonus, I wonder just how fair it is. I have a brother who built himself a house last year. He could not benefit from this $500 subsidy, but if I were to build myself a home this winter, I could get it. How can the minister maintain that this is fair and just? After all, that amount of $500 was taken from the pockets of Canadian taxpayers through the levy of taxes in general. Is this really fair? It may have encouraged housing construction over a longer period and a spread over a 12 month rather than an eight month period, but that program does not change the problem at all and in no way increases the number of days or hours of work in the building industry. I had a look at the results it was able to achieve in the Saguenay area, and I could prove to you that those houses built during the winter were merely projects which would have been carried out in summer and were undertaken a few months ahead of time.
Therefore, not a single additional hour of work was provided by this formula in the area. I believe the same thing goes for many other regions.
Another matter I should like to deal with is unemployment insurance. In our capacity as members of parliament, we are in some way the father-confessors of people who come to us with their problems. In regard to unemployment insurance, I must in all fairness pay tribute to the majority of the employees of that department, especially to those of the local office in my riding, for the manner in which they discuss things over with those who consult them.
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, there is a rather sensitive point I would like to deal with. Workers are not lawyers in general. It would be uncommon to find lawyers among them. Therefore, they do not know how the act is applied. They cannot interpret all the regulations of an act and I would even say that the great majority of workers know nothing about the Unemployment Insurance Act.

Obviously, the government should not be blamed for that, and I do not intend to blame them. Nevertheless, I wonder whether it could not be possible to undertake some program to educate the working class through unions, the employment office or unemployment insurance offices. I wonder also whether or not a way could be found to publish a pamphlet summing up in language workers would easily understand, how the act is applied, what are their actual rights and how they can assert them. The procedure to be followed in connection with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act could then be explained to them in a simplified manner. For my part, I have read two or three times the Unemployment Insurance Act and I must admit that it is not easy to understand its clauses. Therefore, as is the case with any other act, it is hard to interpret.
It refers us from one section to another and finally we have to read three sections at the same time to try to understand part of a section.
In short, it is extremely complicated, and that is why the worker does not understand the act and does not try to understand it in many cases. Consequently, I wonder if the government could not undertake an advertising campaign along the lines I suggested.
What happens, Mr. Chairman, is that the worker who applies for unemployment insurance benefits is unaware of the basic conditions required and fills his application in a way that disqualifies him completely. Two or three weeks later, he receives a letter telling him that he is not eligible for such and such a reason. Of course, he goes to the unemployment office and says: That is not what I meant. And he is answered: But that is what you said.
Thus, because he did not understand the law and was unable to interpret it, the worker is disqualified, sometimes after having paid his unemployment insurance contributions during quite a long period of time.
A case has even come to my knowledge where a man who had paid his contributions to the unemployment insurance fund since its creation was disqualified the first time he applied for benefits. He had paid his contributions through the years, ever since the operation of unemployment insurance, but he was unable to get insurance benefits because, in his application, he made a statement which simply disqualified him.
In short, Mr. Chairman, it seems that one has to be either a lawyer, to know the legisla-

tion and use it, or a liar and be able to get away with giving a more or less honest answer to the questions that the officials of unemployment insurance offices ask, as they have to-I do not blame the officials for asking those question; they have a job to do and that is their responsibility-because of the drafting of those questions and because of the situation in which the worker who is not used to report to offices finds himself. That is how it happens that the worker gives answers which disqualify him.
That is why I ask the Minister of Labour whether it would not be possible to undertake an education program concerning the applications for unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Chairman, that was about all the remarks I had to make on the estimates of the Department of Labour.
To sum it up, I should like to point out to the minister that there is still much to be done in that field to meet general requirements.
I think that improvements have been made. The minister indicated that there is a labour code being prepared and that very soon, we will have to discuss a revision of the whole labour legislation.
This is of course a very complex field. We must take into consideration quite a large number of economic or psychological factors. But I think it would be a good thing if the government, as soon as possible and with the co-operation of all organizations involved, were to see to it that this code which will govern the administration of labour legislation within the framework of federal jurisdiction is drafted in clearer terms.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks on the estimates of the Department of Labour will be brief.
First I want to congratulate the minister for the huge task he has achieved.
I know that he endeavours with all his might to solve problems which today are facing the whole country, and other nations as well. Indeed, the labour problem is one which requires a more and more serious and thorough study, so that definite solutions might be found, which seems impossible within the present structure of our economic and political system.
I know that various programs have been developed, especially in the last ten years, to solve the problem of winter unemployment. By various publicity campaigns and the application of some legislation, there have been endeavours to remedy as far as possible the plague of winter unemployment.
Supply-Labour
There were agreements made with the provinces to promote winter works at the municipal level. This experience has been going on for a few years.
Several municipalities experienced this method and they have come to the conclusion that this was certainly not the most efficient formula, because it created rather complicated financial problems for them. Some municipalities no longer dare resort to this method to help their people, because they encounter too many complications and the burden in the final analysis falls on the shoulders of taxpayers, and property owners, in turn, complain that this situation is not for the best.
Of course, they tried another formula, last year, in order to encourage home building.
They maintain, according to the report that was issued, that out of 32,000 applications, more than 24,000 were accepted, whereby the owners building during the December-March period qualified for the $500 bonus. I am wondering whether they can really boast about the efficiency of the $500 bonus. I am sure that out of the 32,000 applications, thousands of homes would have been built during the winter, even without this legislation. Employment possibilities may have been increased or facilitated, but I do not believe it was really a performance to boast about as regards the solving of the winter employment problem.
On the other hand, in the field of home building, it must be admitted that, during the summer, according to builders and suppliers of building materials, there has been a decline in the building of private homes compared to the increases of the past years, because the demand is being held down not by the lack of a real need for new homes, but by the financing capabilities of various institutions established in order to assist in the building of homes, such as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and of the prospective owners themselves.
Therefore, it cannot be said that those palliatives are a solution to the problem we have to face, and which will become more and more difficult, if we go on, in the context of today's economy, linking the rights of the consumers, and of human beings to obtain the essentials of life-like food, clothing, housing and even those things that are considered a luxury in certain cases-to the sole criteria of work. Those days are gone forever.
Automation was briefly mentioned by the Minister of Labour, when he said that he will make another statement later today on

Supply-Labour
the subject. As regards this problem which baffles us today, economists serving the presidents or economic organizations in the United States alleged, a lew months ago, in a statement to the press, as well as in recommendations to the American congress, that automation should be studied in a concrete and precise manner, because the American economy will have to meet problems still more serious than the post-war ones.
We are going through a century of rapid development, where production techniques are forced upon us to such an extent that we sometimes hardly know where to turn to find a solution. In order to do this, we try enacting legislation, for instance with regard to the rehabilitation of the unemployed by technical training, but people do not seem to realize that, in the twentieth century, it becomes increasingly possible to produce essential goods, services and even modern comfort while liberating more and more people from manual labour.
The tendency is rather to multiply the positions, to try and create new jobs by all possible means, while more and more efforts should be made to free human beings, in this technical age which can produce faster and better, with the quick production we experienced in the twentieth century, besides meeting human needs.
It is mostly along those lines that the remarks I intend to make must be considered.
Our universities now graduate experts in the fields of space development, technical methods and applications, in all production fields. Even large corporations, the powerful economic interests, under the leadership of private enterprise, hire experts, pay bonuses to their own employees in order to find solutions likely to improve the means of production in their own plants. This will necessarily bring about after a few years, when those suggestions are implemented, the dismissal of their own fellow workers.
Under the pressure of labour unions, working hours have been reduced. As recently as 25 or 30 years ago, the labour class had still to work 60 or 65 hours a week, while today the burden of factory workers has been reduced by approximately 50 per cent, as far as working hours are concerned.
The same thing happens in the field of farm production. Through commercial farms, the setting up of larger and larger farms, new production techniques are continually developed. In that same field, production techniques were also developed by all kinds of technical, scientific and progressive proce-
[Mr. Perron.)
dures in order to free human beings from work.
Therefore, I wonder whether the time has not come for the Minister of Labour to ask the government to set up a commission especially instructed, in co-operation with other departments, to seek the development of programs that would provide, not full employment, but especially security for all, a well thought-out security, consistent with the tremendous production capacity of this country.
We are fortunate in having as neighbour a country where science and modern techniques are developed to the highest possible level. We, in Canada, have access to the scientific know-how of that country. Our young nation, Canada, with a population of barely 20 million people, with almost infinitely diversified resources, in the ground and underground, with an industrious population, as we proved it during the last war, had no unemployment problem during the years 1939-45. All those who were able to fill some kind of a job, civilian or military, were given work. There was no problem. There was no need to set up a Senate committee made up of members of parliament to study the ill effects of unemployment in Canada during those years.
So now, in peacetime, is it not abnormal to find such a large number of people deprived of the necessaries of life for lack of a job, while warehouses throughout the country are overflowing with consumer goods?
I suggest, therefore, that we must turn to solutions other than devices such as winter works as applied to housing or post office construction throughout Canada.
I do not think this can really provide us with a worth-while solution to deal with the problem now facing the Canadian parliament and hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
Time and time again, during those last ten years when the two governments have been in office, we have been given statistical data on unemployment.
Let us examine the unemployment figures for Canada. Quebec still leads the rest of the country with over 100,000 unemployed, and this in a province claiming to be in full development, supposedly going through a quiet revolution, in short, in a province where some ministers are paying lip service to cooperative federalism.
No solution has really been found to the problem of poverty amid plenty, to the problem of workers who are unemployed today.

Whether it be through lack of technical training, the trained or untrained unemployed is nevertheless a human being who, in many cases, is head of a family, with three, four, five mouths to feed; he does not believe in those far fetched formulas causing him to be idle over the last ten or 15 years, from the end of the war until now.
Is it not time a social security program were considered, conceived and implemented, in order to meet the needs of the Canadian people, in accordance with the opportunities provided by the economic potential of Canada?
Mr. Chairman, there is not a single minister or hon. member here who sincerely wonders whether, in six or 12 months from now, we will have enough consumer goods to meet the needs of a population of 18 or 19 million. Nobody worries about that because we are all convinced of our tremendous production potential and, at the same time, of our possibilities in the field of foreign trade. In fact, we can easily sell to other countries the consumer goods we produce, but nobody worries about our surpluses in various fields.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the efforts made by all of us here to find solutions to our present problems, thousands of Canadians are wary about the future and wonder if we will be able to meet our obligations, considering the lack of employment opportunities in our industries. In fact, it must be remembered that numerous Canadian workers are being laid off on account of new production techniques.
In the province of Quebec, certain plants which formerly employed 800 to 1,000 people can now double their output with a staff of 300 only.
Of the 600 or 700 people who were laid off, there are maybe 300 or 400 who have been able to get new jobs because of new needs but the 200 or 300 others remain unemployed. The latter may get temporary employment for four or five months in the year. In fact, many of Quebec's unemployed work four or five months a year because they are unable to find jobs which would keep them busy all year round.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard), all possible efforts are being made, in certain quarters, to find answers to those problems through very complex laws, and it is thought that the needs of the unemployed are thus being met. Perhaps those efforts would be successful if it were not necessary in this field, to cope with reserve funds that are always depleted and
Supply-Labour
have to be bolstered by yearly $50 million grants by the Canadian government. It seems that we try, as far as possible, to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds, as the party in office is wont to do.
Attempts are made to save money and to prevent abuses by those who are not entitled or who would be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, by passing complicated laws, and by creating situations whereby the applicants practically disqualify themselves from unemployment insurance benefits.
Formalities are getting more complicated than ever and investigations upon investigations are being made. At first attempts are made to obtain and even to suggest to some extent an answer from the person being investigated.
The unemployed is asked whether he would like to work in his own locality to which he answers "yes", which is quite normal. So, it is jotted down on his card that he wishes to work in his own locality.
Subsequently, a suggestion is made to him, and the answer to the following question is practically put in his mouth: "What salary would you accept? About $40 or $50 a week?" The applicant of course will not reply: "I am prepared to work for $18 or $20 a week". He will say: "Yes, $45 or $50 a week would be fine".
And then, after two or three weeks, he receives a notice to the effect that his application was rejected under section 52 of the Unemployment Insurance Act because he has stated that he would work only in his own locality. Of course he can appeal to the court of referees; he is even entitled to secure counsel, but at his own expense. More often than not, the poor labourer does not know anything about the numerous regulations which today are no longer a summary of the act as it was passed and which has been consolidated in 10, 12 and even 15 volumes. In fact, the act is so complicated that unemployment officers have to get legal advice in order to interpret every section of the act or its regulations which today are consolidated in a certain number of volumes and which baffle the layman.
Then the poor unemployed gets a notice of suspension because his eligibility to unemployment insurance benefits is limited since he stated that he wanted to work in his own locality.
Four weeks go by and then another reason is found to refuse him benefits. It is claimed that he limited his employment opportunities by requesting a higher salary than the average salary paid in his locality or region,

Supply-Labour
since he stated that he wanted $45, $50 or $60 a week. A way is found to stop his benefits again for another period. And when that is not done, he is offered a low paid job so that, in most cases, after paying some essential expenses out of the weekly salary he could earn in a given locality in his region or county, he would not even be left with $18 or $20 a week.
He is offered a job which, because of the cost or the lack of transportation will require him to keep two homes, that is his home in his locality and room and board which will cost him $25, $30 or even $40; in the end, that job will bring him much less than the unemployment insurance benefits he is entitled to and would normally get. And we are satisfied with increasing the complexity of the various existing acts or to pass new ones.
Much was made of the winter works program and the great number of jobs it would create but we seem to forget today that there are between 250,000 and 300,000 summer unemployed in Canada. As I said many times, summer unemployment, just like winter unemployment, is a serious problem which creates hardship within the family.
Those unemployed people are unable to provide for their family's essential needs. Therefore, is it not about time for us to face the unemployment problem from another angle and to consider employment as a means to cope with abundance, to solve the private or public charity problem or the distress problem, at a time when want and insecurity which are prevailing in many Canadian homes are not due to the lack of production of consumers' goods or of services meant for Canadian citizens?
Mr. Chairman, it is often said that "one must live by the sweat of one's brow". But when the bread is on the table, when it is delivered to our homes, I am wondering whether enough sweat was not accumulated already to enable the human being to eat this bread at least with a little dignity.
Is not the real purpose of production to meet human needs? Also, is not the real function of industry, that of creating employment or producing adequate quantities of goods to satisfy human needs?
Let us stop requiring private enterprise and crown corporations to create employment, since the real function of any human activity should be to allow human beings to live in dignity within society.
We could even make a comparison on this subject. If a man who owned five dogs gave them only one bone to chew on, we can well

imagine the most tremendous dog-fight ever seen. The same situation applies to human beings. Why attempt to create jobs, why centre upon the finding of jobs all our efforts to solve the problem of insecurity in Canada, when work should not necessarily be considered nowadays as essential to ensure adequate production.
If the human mind succeeded in developing methods of producing more easily and more quickly the goods necessary, not only to meet our essential needs, but also to provide comfort to the Canadian people in this twentieth century, those goods should serve a useful purpose.
Our universities have found a way to produce scientists who have not only conquered space but who also know a lot of other things. But the same universities failed to form economists able to set up a system of social security which would meet the needs of human beings.
The field of economics includes also financial and monetary matters, and it is said: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread". In this regard, economists have become theologians and, for 35 or 40 years, those theologians have tormented us with this sentence: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread".
Yesterday, I read in the newspapers of the province of Quebec a letter from the Canadian bishops warning legislators and those who look after the problem of labour management relations to prepare for tomorrow a social security program for the Canadian people and not merely create jobs, because automation is here and we must face it seriously in order to improve the situation for the years to come.
If to manage one must anticipate, I feel that it is time more than ever for the minister to urge his colleagues, especially the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), to set up a commission which would prepare plans for the uplifting of human beings, by enabling them to benefit more widely from our wealth, instead of being offered a stopgap. It is imperative to set up a commission which will plan for the years to come the distribution of wealth to each and every Canadian citizen.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to go into detail respecting the estimates of this department; the hon. member for Ontario, a former minister of labour and a successful one, dealt and has already given a general outline. However, there are

one or two observations that I would make with respect to the general position of unemployment. I recall, when hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting over here, how often the very walls of this chamber shook with the condemnation that was heaped on us because there was unemployment.
They promised an end of unemployment. They promised a new heaven and a new earth in the field of human relations. The minister now gives a statement to the committee in which he has to admit grudgingly that the problem of unemployment has been little improved in the last year and a half; and in that year and a half there has been an expansion, as there was during the days we were in office from 1961 on, when our policies started to work. Those policies which were condemned by the hon. gentlemen who sit opposite, now having been adopted by them, become the cornerstones of the economic development of this country.
They have brought into effect one or two measures-one of which I shall refer to-to meet the unemployment problem; but generally speaking they have taken no action whatsoever in this connection. The legislation placed on the statute books between 1957 and 1963, including the vocational training schools act, has been carried on. Despite an economic improvement in North America, we still have a very large measure of unemployment. We were told they had the solution. No longer does it appear in the press as being a serious problem, despite the fact that hundreds of thousands are still unemployed.
Those who sit in the front benches today had the answers during the period 1957 to 1963. It was folly, they said, on our part to compare unemployment in Canada with that in the United States, where the same situation prevailed, where unemployment ran very high, and where, despite all the efforts of economists and leaders in government, unemployment mounted and was approximately on the same level as Canada's, with the exception of course that we have peculiar and serious climatic conditions in the winter.
They were unable to place before you, Mr. Chairman, anything which they had done; they merely adopted the policies of the former government which they had condemned. I am not going to go into the pegging of the dollar, but I can never forget the counterfeit currency which was distributed across Canada to indicate a serious economic condition in Canada and to draw attention to the claim that what we had done was detrimental
Supply-Labour
to the country. Today it is the cornerstone. The heresy of yesterday is the Liberal orthodoxy of today in this connection.
Now, what has the government done? True enough, there has been economic change for the better in North America. One has only to read the United States press. There has been a very considerable economic development in the last year and a half. But we have problems which this government refuses to face. They are problems which must be faced if the question of employment is to be met and assured and Canada's national growth is to continue. These problems face us and we find our trade position with imports exceeding exports. With bankruptcies greater than they have been for many years, with agriculture, at least in the central and maritime provinces, suffering very severely and thereby detrimentally affecting not only our economy but also the employment situation, the government spends its time trying to secure passage of a resolution to provide for a flag. Last night they had the opportunity to bring in legislation, which is not ready and has not been prepared, but they chose to vote against being given that opportunity.
One matter which was boasted about was the $500 bonus for winter building. We are told that was a success. We are told that it brought unusual development, and therefore jobs. We have said it was not a success. We have said that what it actually did was to transfer building construction from one part of the year to another, to the detriment of the consumer or householder. I should like to quote as a supporting witness in this connection the hon. member for York East. He is an experienced builder. He was of those, along with the hon. member for Essex South, who in a recent television program revealed their thinking, exposed their hearts and spoke with frankness. I should like to refer to what the experienced builder had to say. He deals with the fact that a number of private members of parliament are not being considered by the present government. Both of these hon. members to whom I have referred said that. Then he said something to this effect: "We are all considered as privates and they think they are colonels". Mr. Chairman, I have never seen that relationship but apparently it exists. Then the hon. member for York East spoke of the difficulties under which these hon. members operate. Take, for example this question of the $500 winter bonus. He said:
-let us suppose that I had something to do with national housing and that I was on the committee
to advise.

He has not and he was not. but he said "suppose". He went on:
I would have advised them-
I think that must be the Minister of Labour.
-immediately that the $500 winter bonus is absolutely useless-*
When the evidence is given by an experienced member supporting the government, Mr. Chairman, its importance cannot be overemphasized.
-because having been in the business and knowing what the cost of winter construction is, knowing that most builders would rather give you $500 than to build a house in the wintertime. I could have told them that and saved embarrassment, because with the great boom of construction, $500 purports to be the reason. It is not the reason at all.
I think the Minister of Labour, when he is looking around for experts, might just have a whispered conversation with the hon. member for York East, who is experienced in such matters. He goes on:
It is not the reason at all. The reason is that there is a feeling of expansion.
I need go no further, Mr. Chairman, to answer the minister and any other ministers who speak so fulsomely of this $500 winter bonus scheme, than to quote the words of the hon. member for York East, who tells us on the basis of experience that he knows what he is talking about, but that the minister does not.
It is an amazing revelation, Mr. Chairman. Those two hon. members were away from the whip on that day and spoke with great authority. I was amazed to hear one hon. member say that so difficult is it for these ministers to carry on that the minister of defence, when he produced the white paper, wrote it in longhand.
Then he said:
He did not even trust It to be typed by the establishment.
These are not the revelations of members of the opposition, Mr. Chairman. These are the considered opinions of members supporting the government, men who have had experience. Would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question? Is he aware of the fact that most congratulations which I received on how accurate I was came from members of his party?

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member ever got commendation for anything I do not mind his boasting about it, because I have never seen any reason why he should. I say that in the kindness of spirit to one who at all times is the essence of affability.
You have not heard him in caucus.
If the hon. gentleman has a question, I do not mind.

No, I am sorry; I should not have interrupted. The right hon. gentleman said that the hon. member is always the essence of affability, and I could not resist the temptation to say: "You should hear him in caucus".

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, I did not get the interruption, but I know it was a semi-judicial pronouncement and one with which I am sure I would not agree.
I am simply pointing out that the $500 bonus scheme was no good, and the only member on the other side of the house who knows anything about building, according to what was said on this broadcast, says that it was worthless and he would not have established it if he had had anything to do with the matter.
What has the government done to meet the unemployment situation? Simply continued the policies of the past, with one or two stunts such as the $500 bonus; but I am not going to deal with that any more because it was dealt with so well and effectively by the hon. member. How are we going to meet this problem? When we said that automation made greater unemployment inevitable and that it would take time in order to produce the necessary skills and training for men and women to be able to operate modern machinery, we were ridiculed. The plan that was brought into effect by the hon. member for Ontario when he was minister of labour will be a monument throughout the years to the wisdom and the capacity of that hon. member. He brought into being a plan that provides for the training of over 100,000 Canadians a year to enable them to carry out the responsibilities of operating difficult machinery.
That brings me to another phase in connection with this department. Mention has already been made of the Norris report. I was amazed that one of the trustees admitted he had never read the report in full. One of the maritime trustees, whose responsibility it is to carry out the principles inherent in

that report, had not read the report in question. The rest of us have read that report and it is a report that will be a must for all who would understand the developments in the S.I.U.
What has the government done about it? They appointed a board of trustees. That board of trustees has not yet been brought before a committee of parliament. Questions are asked and we are told the committee is to meet at some time in the future. I want to get the assurance from the minister that these trustees are going to appear before a committee now, not next fall, not next winter, but now. Many questions have related to the administration of the maritime board of trustees. Answers have not been given. The attitude of the minister has simply been that ultimately the members of the board or a member will come before a committee of parliament.
One of the recommendations had to do with Hal Banks and also with McLaughlin who today occupies the top position in the S.I.U. Read that report. Imagine Mr. Millard saying he had not read it. Is that the reason that McLaughlin, who was condemned in almost as strong terms as Banks, still occupies the number one position, the controlling position, in the S.I.U.? Is it because a member of the board has not read the report that the same old list still exists, with the result that from time to time decent, respectable seamen come to members of parliament and point out that they cannot break through the wall, that they are on the no ship list? What is the reason for this? Why does the board of maritime trustees permit these conditions to continue? Why cannot we have any information about the arrangements that were made between Mr. Hall of the S.I.U. and the Canadian government or the board of trustees?
What about Banks? One cannot speak of him without referring to his absence from the demands of justice. Yes, they prosecuted him for conspiracy.
And kissed him goodbye.

Over the years he had been one of the pally boys of the Liberal party. Whenever he was in difficulty somehow or other an order in council could be passed to relieve him from being removed from our country. When he was prosecuted 20220-486

Sir, the record of the government in connection with Banks is one of the highest negligence, and worse. They prosecuted him. He was let out on bail. Your Honour knows that one of the first principles of a bail bond, as set forth in all bail bonds, except on an appeal in which case it may be inserted, is that the person involved does not depart the said court without leave. According to newspaper reports an order was made by the chief justice of Quebec granting bail to Mr. Banks. I wonder whether the terms of that recognizance include a condition which would prevent Mr. Banks from leaving Canada?
The member for Bow River wondered whether this would be the course followed. If there was no solicitude for Banks, Mr. Chairman, there was certainly negligence in dealing with Banks. When an ordinary man is arrested, charged with an offence and enters into a bond he has to undertake not to leave the jurisdiction. But Banks, with a five year sentence hanging over him, could sign a bond for $25,000 which, to use a vulgarism, is just peanuts in that league, without a provision that he must not leave Canada, he being a United States citizen.
We followed this matter throughout and asked questions. On July 27 and succeeding days we asked the government over and over again what they were going to do about the matter. The government did nothing. Banks disappeared. We have been trying to get information for weeks with regard to what is being done to find Banks. I believe that the reason the government does not give us any information is that the government knows that Banks cannot be extradited on the charge of conspiracy, with regard to which he was out on bail, and he certainly cannot be extradited on the other charges, one of contempt of court and the other a further charge of conspiracy yet to be tried.
Here is the interesting part. The law officers of the crown and special counsel allowed this man out on bail when they must have known that if he walked over into the United States he could stay clear of any danger of being apprehended. This is, to me, the most ridiculous thing that has ever happened in connection with Canadian justice.

Supply-Labour
Ordinarily I would not use the expression, but one of the great supporters of the Liberal party, the Toronto Daily Star said, on August 19, "Mr. Banks thumbs his nose".
Hal Banks seems to be thumbing his nose successfully at Canadian justice.
He is. Any one of the law officers must have known that you could not extradite him if he got across the line. What a commentary upon the administration of justice upon which we in this country pride ourselves. Here is a man who comes into the country, disregards our laws in connection with immigration status as no one else could do, is prosecuted and let out on a bail bond that will not be effective because it does not prevent him from leaving the jurisdiction of the court.

May I ask the hon. member a question because I am interested in this? I should like to ask the hon. member if he can say, from his legal knowledge and as a former prime minister, whether or not it is possible for a person in Canada, under indictment and on bail, to leave Canada without there being a record with immigration or other authorities?
I have never tried to leave Canada that way, and neither has the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Have you ever been out on bail?
No; but the bail bond did not prevent his doing what he did. This is a very good question.
This is a very serious question. Is it possible for a person to cross the line under these circumstances without the Canadian or United States authorities having a record of his doing so?

I can only say that the hon. gentleman's question indicates that it could not be. I cannot disagree with the apparent conclusion that he has in mind, having regard to the nature of his question, that Mr. Banks crossed the line into the United States. When he did so, they would say, "Canadian or American?" They would not require an answer, perhaps, but when the name Banks was given they would know him. Even if the name was not given as Hal Banks, if you had seen him once you would never forget him.
Is this man in the United States? Here is an interesting thing, Mr. Chairman. Weeks after the event I asked the minister if he had ascertained from the immigration officers of the United States whether or not he entered

there. He said, I will make inquiries. One newspaper reported that a minister had said within the last few days Banks was in New York. He does not need to conceal himself. In my opinion, he cannot be extradited. Having first read the Extradition Act, I then made inquiries from other counsel and they told me they cannot believe it possible that he could be brought back to Canada. Is that the reason we get the kind of supercilious answer we receive when we ask this question?-"We have spoken to the F.B.I. in the United States." Imagine a criminal who flouted every law he could flout according to the Norris report, convicted and given five years-how he must laugh at the administration of Canadian justice. Already there is evidence in the United States that people are asking why it is that Canadian justice, which has always had the highest reputation, should have allowed itself to be circumvented in this way. Why can we not get any answers?
Sir, here is a man with a record of violence who, after conviction in September, I believe, came to Ottawa. The law officers did not pick him up then, they charged him with that offence later for which he will face trial. Why would a government that was anxious to get its hands on Banks fail for five long weeks to ascertain from United States immigration authorities whether or not he had gone into the United States? This is not only a frightful commentary, but one for which responsibility rests on the government. I say that without any fear of successful contradiction. They do not seem to want him. They go through the motions. They let him out on bail. I am not arguing that; the court did that. They let him out on a bail bond to which they could have objected.
An ordinary man suspected of crime cannot leave the jurisdiction of a court. Banks, convicted of a crime, could and apparently did. This is one of the great mysteries of our times. He never had anything to worry about. The trials meant nothing to him because he must have known when those trials started that so long as he was able to get back to his own country, whatever the penalties might be in Canada, they would not be imposed if a bail bond were provided. He had nothing to worry about, nothing whatever.
Sir, we want to get to the bottom of this. I asked for an investigation and the answer given by the government was, you do not need an investigation. I am beginning to think that is right. It is as obvious as the nose on one's face that if he were not extraditable, if he were convicted of con-

spiracy and allowed to go out on bail under a bond that did not prevent leaving the jurisdiction, this would provide him with an opportunity of which he was not slow to take advantage. I warned about that in May and in July. The answer I received from the Minister of Justice in July, I believe it was, was that we have a sufficient guarantee he will be in court on September 14 to take his trial. Well, it is a great mystery. The boss of the S.I.U. in the past can still exercise that authority through his vice president. The boss, convicted of a serious crime, subject to what the Supreme Court of Canada may do on appeal, is able to walk out of this country, drive out or leave in any other way, fly from any responsibility and simply vanish, and I say he vanished without there being any apparent concern on the part of the government.
The Minister of Justice, in a very suave way, indicates that we have got hopes that we will get him. You do not bring honour to the administration of Canadian justice by allowing a wrongdoer, a gangster, to act as he will, to dominate as he feels, and then when he faces the law, when he loses, to escape entirely.
I come back to the question of investigation. The government of Canada, despite the very lucid circumstances connected with this matter, owes it to the people of Canada to give an opportunity for examination into the looseness with which this man played with the law of Canada. At the same time the other, who is to face a charge of conspiracy with Banks, I think on September 14, is still in the seats of the mighty

McLaughlin.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg asked a very simple question as to whether anybody had inquired from the S.I.U. where Banks was as he received his salary cheque from the S.I.U. Mr. Chairman, I believe that they never thought of that across the way. Do you? They would have had an awful shock if they had thought of asking that question. This is one of the most serious things the government has permitted to take place, to make a laughingstock of justice, to place a foreign gangster in a position where he can well boast in the United States how he achieved his objectives, broke the law, was convicted, and served outside of jail in another country, the land of his birth.
This Banks' record has left a legacy to the S.I.U. that must be discharged, and we want to know whether it is being discharged. We find these seamen who state that they are being denied jobs because of a do not ship list. The minister says there is none that he 20220-486i
Supply-Labour
knows of. This is something that requires to be looked into.
There are many things that separate us that often are of no great consequence but, sir, when you find the law of the land trampled on and made ridiculous, the mystery of Hal Banks deserves to be looked into. I am not going over what I said before, but for years he was the anointed of Liberalism. When he could have been deported for smuggling- any other person would have been-an order in council was passed by the St. Laurent government to give him landed status, and it omitted his conviction.
When he came into Canada he had a record. Sometimes I have felt that some portions of the imprisonment imposed on him were not just-14 years for the issuing of bouncing cheques seems to me to be beyond what is within the realm of reason, but that was his sentence and, lo and behold, when he came to Canada the immigration officers forgot to enter that he had a record, or he could not have gotten in. Then when he established another record in Canada, when the order in council was made the Liberal government of that day forgot to include the conviction. In 1964 they forgot to get a forwarding address.

In view of the emphasis the Leader of the Opposition has placed on this matter of Hal Banks and the S.I.U. and the points he has brought to the attention of the committee, I would like to ask if in his opinion there should be a request made for a complete and an exhaustive examination as to how a man having a criminal record in the United States was allowed into Canada, how a man having broken the law of Canada on smuggling and being convicted, and having broken that law again, has now escaped from Canada-how all this could occur from beginning to end unless there is a suspicion of conspiracy? Is the right hon. member prepared to state in view of his own remarks that this is a matter into which members of the House of Commons have a right to demand a complete and exhaustive examination?
It is, exactly. I am not accepting the principle of conspiracy-I am not dealing with that; but I would like to see an investigation all through the past-
From 1957?

From three or four months before he came to Canada, and the correspondence from then on with the officials.

Supply-Labour
We tried to get rid of him when we were in office.
Oh, oh.
Look at the record. But he had landed rights and an order in council that gave him those rights and we could not deport him. Otherwise we would have.
Will the right hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

I ask the question because I am quite sure the right hon. gentleman would not wish to be misunderstood. Did I understand him correctly when he said that the Minister of Justice had stated that there was no list?
Yes, that he knew of no list. Yes, that is what I said.

Does the right hon. gentleman not recall that the statement of the Minister of Labour was that he had been assured by the chairman of the maritime commission, a distinguished member of the supreme court of my province-that he had the assurance of this eminent justice, the chairman of the commission, that there was no list?

I do not doubt you
had an assurance. But you can have an assurance, and the man who is out of a job and who cannot get one because he was on the black list knows whether there was a list or not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have just heard the Leader of the Opposition making certain references to what he calls the mystery of Hal Banks. But perhaps the greatest mystery, when we remember that this occurred in 1957, and that the facts were known to the former government, is why he was not brought to justice earlier. Why did they do nothing about Hal Banks until 1961, when the seaway had been physically blocked by the contending parties? That is the great mystery about this. I should like an answer to that question, and I am sure the country would like one as well.
The Leader of the Opposition also made certain assertions about the legal process and the practice of the courts. I am sure he would not want to mislead the house with regard to what I think are principles generally accepted by lawyers. First, he asserted that there had been negligence on the part of the law officers of the crown in permitting Banks to go free on bail.
No. I never said that. I said in letting him go free on bail without the inclusion of the words "shall not depart the court without leave".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I appreciate the right hon. gentleman's intervention and I would refer him specifically to form 28 of the Canadian Criminal Code and the subsection contained in that form which specifically excepts from the provisions with regard to bail on appeal the words which he has used. Some months ago in this house the hon. member for Bow River made an assertion that this was a customary and standard inclusion in any form of bail bond. I point out now, as I did then, that that is entirely false. It is not a provision of the Criminal Code and I am advised by the senior counsel acting for the crown in this case that it is not the practice of the courts in Quebec to insert that provision in bail bonds, and that such a provision could not have been expected in this case. I emphasize again that the request of the law officers of the crown to the court was that Mr. Banks should not be allowed out on bail at all but that he should be kept in custody. But I would also remind hon. members that it is, after all, up to the judge to decide in what circumstances a man should be allowed bail, and it was the judgment of Mr. Justice Tremblay, the chief justice of Quebec that he should be granted this privilege. It is a damaging and misleading statement to suggest that the law officers of the crown were responsible for letting Banks out on bail. Decisions as to bail are, after all, the duty of the court. Moreover, it is the duty of the Minister of Justice, as well as the rest of us, to respect the decisions of the courts, and that is what we are doing.
The decision in accordance with the Criminal Code was that this man should be set at liberty. I do not know what the right hon. gentleman's concept of liberty is, but one would gather from him that he believes it means keeping a man under 24 hour surveillance and taking him into custody if he makes one move outside his house. That is not the law of this country, and I hope it will never be. I am surprised that the Leader of the Opposition should suggest, in any way, that it should be. All appropriate steps had been taken by the law officers of the crown to lay all possible charges against Hal Banks. The prosecution was pressed as soon as possible, and a conviction was secured. Proceedings were taken to make certain that Banks would be available for the hearing-
Where is he?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me point out again to hon. members who would like to muddy the record that it was a decision of the Quebec courts exercising their jurisdiction that he should be allowed liberty. We have heard too often in this house the suggestion that in some way or other the decision of the court should have been disregarded and that this prisoner, or any prisoner, if let out on bail should be subjected to surveillance. It would be a mockery of justice if the law officers of the crown were to disregard orders of the court, specifically that a man should be allowed out at liberty.
I should like to reply to two questions-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps before the right hon. gentleman replies to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice I should bring to his attention and to the attention of all hon. members that our debate in committee this afternoon seems to have strayed away from the labour aspect of this situation. I realize it is not easy to determine what part of this matter involves justice and what part involves labour. But I would remind hon. members who will take part in the debate from now on that they should try to address their remarks to the estimates of the Department of Labour.

I was trying so hard to do just what Your Honour has suggested. But you, yourself, have made apparent the difficulty of deciding where the Department of Justice ends and the Department of Labour begins. That is one of the great difficulties in this case. There are two departments involved. If I tried to bring this matter up on the estimates of the Department of Justice, the answer would be-the Norris commission.
But to answer the hon. gentleman, there was no suggestion that the person convicted should not be let out on bail so long as it was assured he would be there to take his punishment. No one suggested there should be any onus on the part of the crown to watch a person as he went from place to place while he was free. What I did suggest was this- that it is a strange commentary on the administration of justice that a gangster who has a sentence of five years should be free to go as he will to the United States or any other place, yet if a man who has a good record in the past is charged with an offence and let out on bail, the provision made in respect of him is as follows-I will read the form:
Supply-Labour
Whereas by order dated the-day of-reciting that A.B., hereinafter called the accused, was charged before me for a certain offence herein mentioned, and that-
I am sorry. I have been reading from the wrong form.
Oh.

They both appear on the same page. This is the one. This is form 28.
The condition of the written recognizance is such that whereas the accused was this day charged before the justices within mentioned for that-
And here appear details of the charge
-if, therefore, the accused appears at the next superior court of criminal jurisdiction (or court of general or quarter sessions of the peace) to be holden in and for the said county and there surrenders himself into the custody of the keeper of the common gaol (or lock-up house), and pleads to such indictment as may be found against him by the grand jury, for and in respect to the charge aforesaid, and takes his trial upon the same, and does not depart the said court without leave, then the said recognizance to be void, otherwise to stand in full force and virtue.
Talk about travesties. A man who had committed no known offence, but a prima facie case of the crown has been made out against him, cannot leave the jurisdiction of the courts. But if he had about him the halo of Banks, he can. I have nothing to say about the decision of the court to grant bail. The crown asked for high bail. The judge fixed it at $25,000. But what I do say is that it had the appearance of being more than coincidence that the solicitude for Banks shown during the years still continues, when the bail bond was made out.
The hon. gentleman asked: why did we not prosecute him? As a matter of fact, we set up the Norris commission. That commission found the evidence, and then this government prosecuted on the basis of the evidence the Norris commission brought out.
With reluctance.

I would not like to say that; I would say, after undue delay. Indeed, I do not forget that the former minister of justice, the predecessor of the present minister, withheld action on the warrant for Banks' arrest when he was available to be arrested.

This is a very important point, Mr. Chairman, and I think it ought to be underlined. The incident for which Mr. Banks was convicted occurred in 1957. It occurred after the right hon. gentleman became prime minister of Canada. No new facts

Supply-Labour
were uncovered subsequent to the Norris commission.
Oh, yes.

These facts were investigated at the time and were made known to the government of the day. It was open to that government for all those years to prosecute Mr. Banks for an incident that took place in August, 1957. That is one mystery that I would like to have cleared up by the Leader of the Opposition. Why did he annoint and coddle Mr. Banks and refuse to prosecute him on facts that were known in August, 1957 and widely publicized at that time?
Mr. Chairman, the statement that we refused to prosecute is as completely without foundation as is possible.
It is a fact.

It is unjustified, and
untrue.
It is a fact.
And it is untrue, if a fact can be untrue.
Mr. Chairman, will the Leader of the Opposition deny that this case was investigated by the R.C.M. Police at that time? Will he deny that? He cannot deny it.

I can understand the heated feelings that are aroused in the minister by the revelation of these facts. The way in which this government uses smokescreens such as this to cover up their negligence in connection with Banks is equal only to the solicitude shown throughout the years to him.
Mr. Chairman, would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question?
The evidence was forthcoming-
Would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question?

-in the Norris report. Mr. Chairman, I have never known two to speak at once, and one intelligently; and I am speaking intelligently. I can understand the feeling in this regard. While we argue and the government defends what took place, Banks enjoys his liberty at the expense of the reputation of Canadian justice.
