Mr. Chairman, there are two things with which I should like the Leader of the Opposition to deal. Will he deny that the incident which took place in

1957 was investigated at that time by the police? Will he deny that? Second, will he deny that these facts were made known to the government of the day?

Mr. Chairman, I immediately deny the second question, and as far as the first is concerned, my recollection is that we did everything we could to be sure that if we prosecuted, we would have a case. It was not until Mr. Justice Norris investigated this matter for months and months that sufficient evidence became available-because these employees of the S.I.U. would not talk; they dare not talk; they had hanging over them the tyranny of Banks, and McLaughlin too, and they were afraid to talk and bring out the necessary corroborative evidence.

The Leader of the Opposition has now made it quite clear that this case was investigated in 1957. He has made it quite clear that at that time the government of the day must have concluded that there were not sufficient grounds for prosecution. The evidence upon which Mr. Banks was convicted was not drawn in any way from the Norris report, not at all; it was drawn from evidence collected by the special counsel who were appointed subsequently on the recommendation of Mr. Justice Norris. Mr. Justice Norris asked that special counsel be appointed to investigate all the activities of Mr. Banks. This government appointed those special counsel; they undertook the investigation, with the assistance of the police, and sufficient evidence was accumulated tc secure a conviction. It was open to the Leader of the Opposition in 1957, as head of the government, to instruct that special counsel be appointed to secure the evidence with regard to an event that took place when he was prime minister. But the fact is that the government of that day failed to take action, and it is as a result of action taken by this government that Mr. Banks was convicted.
And he is free.
Where is he now?

Mr. Chairman, I can understand the heated argument the Minister of Labour is putting up in respect of this matter. But if we look at the Norris commission report we will see it was recommended there that special counsel be appointed by the government to look into the evidence submitted to the Norris commission.
No.

That was in order to ascertain whether a charge could be laid as a result of the evidence submitted to the Norris commission and to see whether proper evidence could be brought out in order to prosecute. It was only after the Norris commission report came out and that recommendation was made that we pressed the government to appoint these counsel. It was months afterwards that counsel made a report, and it was months afterwards that the revelations of the report were made and action, based on the prodding of the opposition, was taken to prosecute. This was based on the recommendation that there was enough evidence in the Norris commission report to justify proceeding with the laying of charges.
Then they helped him across the line, too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, first I would confirm what the Minister of Labour said-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -that the previous minister of justice, the minister of justice of the former government, had before him substantially the evidence upon which Banks was convicted in 1963.
Substantially.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That government failed to take action on it. Therefore it does not lie with them to accuse anyone of being dilatory or a friend of Banks. They failed to follow up the evidence that was before their noses. Second, Mr. Chairman, there was another misrepresentation from the other side of the house. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition very solemnly read to the committee a part of the Criminal Code. He started by reading the wrong page, but he got on to the right page.
No; the right page, but the wrong form.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He read to the committee the form of bail bond where an accused is being committed for trial. He was very careful not to read the form used in appeal proceedings such as these, which is subparagraph (g) and which contains nothing like the provisions he read to the committee. There is no provision in that appeal bail bond form set out in the Criminal Code preventing the accused from leaving the jurisdiction or requiring him to remain continuously within the jurisdiction of the court before the day set for the appeal.
Supply-Labour
Where is Banks? Where is your buddy?
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word about automation and manpower consultative services.
Oh, oh.

I would like to comment on the words of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition when he referred to Hal Banks and said he was anointed of Liberalism. I wonder what protection the anointed of Liberalism had under Conservatism, because it took some years before he was brought to court. Certainly the evidence upon which Mr. Banks was convicted is only one aspect of the Norris commission report. There are other matters that were certainly brought to the attention of the government. There was the agreement between a shipping company of Sarnia and the S.I.U. which Mr. Justice Norris considered was in defiance of the law. This matter was discussed at the highest echelons of the government at the time of the previous administration, and nothing was done.
Another matter the right hon. gentleman mentioned was the $500 bonus for winter home building. He quoted the hon. member for York East as a builder. I think if he moved around the construction workers of York South and ascertained that for the first time in many years there was a higher rate of employment during those dour months, he would understand why there is wide support for the very successful enterprise carried on by this government in order to encourage winter employment.
I was very much impressed with the report of the American council on education with regard to the state of employment in the United States. They pointed out that while there were five million unemployed in the United States, there were four million unfilled job opportunities. We are moving into a period when more and more the employment demand will be for skilled personnel. Unskilled people without training, people with deficiencies in education, will find it more and more difficult to gain employment.
In a speech at Queen's University last May the Minister of Labour pointed out that 90 per cent of the light bulbs and tubes manufactured in the United States, with the exception of picture tubes, are produced by 14 machine operators. This is one aspect of the development of automation which does require skilled personnel and yet displaces a lot of workers. The automobile industry in

Supply-Labour
the United States in 1963 produced seven million cars. The automobile industry in the United States in 1955 also produced seven million cars. But in 1963 the industry produced seven million cars with 17 per cent less labour force. This is an important problem which sets up a challenge that this government must meet. It sets up a challenge in terms of the means of production and distribution, a means which will completely revolutionize our social and economic system. This is based largely on the development of automation and a highly sophisticated production system.
Automation is based on three main components. First of all, there is the self-regulating system. For example, the simple thermostat which one has in one's house is a selfregulating system. Second, there is the electronic computer which stores information and is capable of logical decision making. This has made possible the development of our economy and the use of the many services which otherwise would not be available to us. Yet this highly sophisticated and mature machine, the electronic computer, represents a threat to our society and threatens the jobs of hundreds of thousands of workers. The third component is the highly organized assembly system of laying out work. These three components when placed together are the basis of automation.
Automation requires certain types of materials. The hard substances which we use in our economy today are not easily absorbed in a highly automated assembly. Therefore, automation requires new substances, and science is busily engaged in producing these new substances to feed a highly automated system. Someone pointed out that whereas formerly the consumer would set up demand and would set in motion the process of production by his requirements, today it is the scientist and the engineer who are skilfully engaged in determining what such a system can produce and who are putting into reverse the well known saying and showing, as one wag put it, that invention is becoming the mother of necessity.
What are we in this country doing in order to meet the need for skills, and what are we doing in terms of planning? We have a system of joint training projects to which the Minister of Labour has referred. We have engaged in these systems of training, which are joint programs between the provinces and the federal government, in the 12-month period ending March 31, 287,187 Canadians, Of these, 164,420 were people
[Mr. GelberJ
who were being trained in vocational schools and high schools. That means that out of a labour force of 6,600,000 or more there are only 123,000 people receiving training through the joint programs. Of the 164,000 people who are at school more than half are taking business courses. Although these are important it means that only a small number of people in vocational and high schools are getting the skills necessary to absorb them in the productive mechanism which is so important.
It is my contention that we will never be able to build the schools and engage the people to provide the training which is required, unless more is done. The steps already taken by the government help, and the programs started by the previous government are also of assistance. But in the conception of the total problem it seems to me that we are not sufficiently imaginative and must do more. The greatest school for providing industrial skills is industry itself. Industry has the equipment, the knowhow and the leadership. It seems to me that we must conceive of industry not only as producing commodities but also as producing skills which will upgrade the labour force in this country and make it possible in this twentieth century to meet the challenge of automation. We must do more to give inducements to industry, and we must provide the opportunities to develop skilled tradesmen and craftsmen who are so much demanded by our society.
The program announced by the Minister of Labour some months ago, and which he mentioned again today-the manpower consultative service-is one step toward mobilizing our resources toward meeting this objective. We must look to industry as the most important school for retraining our labour force and as the most important school for giving that capability to our workers to meet the challenge of 1964.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, now that we are back on the estimates of the Department of Labour, I should like to say that I was pleased that the hon. member for Ontario made the reference that he did to William Jenoves, who passed away yesterday. I agree with the hon. member for Ontario that in paying tribute to this man who spent six decades working in the trade union movement we are paying tribute to all those who over the years have helped to build this very important and living aspect of our democratic way of life.

We have a Minister of Labour at the present time who is not only an honourable gentleman; he is also a gentleman. That is our trouble. He is a very fine man and is very charming. In fact, with all his charm and his capacity for making promises it mystifies me that he is still a bachelor. And I am saying that in 1964, a leap year at that. As everyone knows he seems in the labour field to be the epitome of the capacity of the Liberals over the years to make promises, and to make them in such a charming way that we are lulled into believing that they are going to be kept. He did it again today, and this time I hope he not only meant it but that it will come true. He went just as far as he could in saying that before the end of the month of September-and when I questioned him he said he meant 1964- legislation for a national labour code would be on the order paper. I hope I do not sound cynical if I refer to the fact that this is the kind of promise that has been made over and over again. True, this minister has never become quite so specific in terms of time. Thus far he has told us it would come "soon" or "as soon as possible" or "very soon" or "just as soon as we can make it", and so on. I hope that this time he has pinned himself down.
I remind him that, as he well knows, when we were dealing with his estimates last year we were able to pin him down fairly well on November 8, 1963. On that day we were dealing with the estimates of the Department of Labour for last year and we got out of the Minister of Labour what seemed like a promise to bring in a national labour code at this session. I was anxious to pin him down on that, and on a couple of other matters as well, and so on page 4605 of Hansard for November 8, 1963, I referred in particular to three matters, amending the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, a labour code, and doing something about the Unemployment Insurance Act. I asked the minister if he would not summon up his courage and assure us that action would be taken on those three matters during the following session of parliament, namely the session now with us. On page 4605 of Hansard for November 8, 1963, I read this paragraph:

Subject to the approval of a number of other persons directly involved, I have no hesitation in saying that we will want to take action on the Unemployment Insurance Act and the labour code within the time mentioned by my hon. friend.
I interject to say that I thought that was a pretty clear promise that at this session we
Supply-Labour
would get action on those two things, the Unemployment Insurance Act and a national labour code. I continue the quotation:
I would be very rash indeed to give the same kind of assurance with respect to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, because, as at the present time, I have not, nor has my department given the kind of consideration in depth-
That is a great phrase.
-to the proposals put forward to justify my giving an assurance of that kind. However, we will consider these proposals and perhaps at a later date I will be glad to add this particular suggestion to the rather optimistic prospect I have given in connection with the other two.
I found the Minister of Labour so charming and such a gentleman last year that I thought it was a certainty that at this session we would get action on the Unemployment Insurance Act and on a national labour code, and that there was a possibility that we would get action on amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. It is now clear that the only one of these three with regard to which there is any hope so far as this session is concerned is the national labour code. I hope it will be on the order paper shortly and I hope the Minister of Labour will make the strongest representations he can to the Prime Minister, the house leader and those who are responsible for things around here to see to it that we get at that item as soon as possible after it gets on the order paper. I need not take any time discussing what is happening to the business of the house at this session, but it still seems to me that some of our time, no matter what else we may have to deal with, should be spent on other legislation and that this is one of the items that should be got through at this session, no matter what happens.
I hope that the labour code will be a substantial document. I hope that at least it will deal with the ingredients that we discussed last year, the first being a minimum wage. I hope that the provision for a minimum wage in the labour code will not be a pious hope. I trust it will not be something that is flexible, permitting different rates in different parts of the country. I hope the minister is aware of the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress, which for a few years was proposing $1.25 an hour as a minimum wage, decided at its last convention that under today's conditions the minimum should be $1.50 an hour.
I also trust there will be provision in the code for maximum number of hours of work per day, a maximum work week and certain other matters. In particular, I hope the labour

Supply-Labour
code will improve the vacations with pay legislation, which is the only ingredient of a national labour code that we now have on the statute books. As the minister knows, this was not put on the statute books by the Liberals, but by the Conservatives when they were in power a few years ago. In my view the provisions with respect to that matter should be improved along the lines of certain private members' public bills that I have introduced. There should also be provision for statutory holidays with pay.
As I say, I hope that these five ingredients at least will be in the national labour code. It may be that a national labour code is also the place to make certain provisions regarding safety and other matters to protect workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction. As the minister said when he was making his remarks earlier, this is a subject about which some of us have been having a good deal to say for a good many years, but I will not today do as I so often do, pull out the 1919 program of the Liberal party. That is a long way back now, but at any rate let us have implementation at this session of the promises that the present generation of Liberals have made to us.
I also hope the minister will pay some attention to what he said on November 8, 1963, regarding the Unemployment Insurance Act. He led us to believe then that action on that matter at this session was on a parallel with the intended action on the national labour code, but there has been no indication at this session that anything of that nature is in store for us. Likewise, even though his commitment last year was not very strong, we feel that improvements are needed in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. If the minister wonders what the details are, he can find them in the record of the debate on these estimates a year ago.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, said, when we started to prepare for this day's debate we wondered what there was to say that we did not say a year ago. We said it all then and virtually nothing has happened in the meantime, except that the minister has given us the benefit of his charm and has made these promises. A year ago we felt that at least he was coping with some very difficult problems involving a number of disputes and so on that were on his doorstep, and we gave him full marks for the courageous and active way he was coping with them. He earned quite a reputation. Even my hon.
[Hr. Knowles.]
friend, the columnist who sits in front of me was rating him very high in the cabinet of that day; but in the meantime we have to settle for his charm. They are wonderful-
Just for a month.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Just for a month?
You should have more by the end of the month.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I hope the minister is not going to turn his charm off at the end of the month-
Charm, plus.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: -but that we will have something solid in terms of legislation.
No LaMarshian stuff.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
But even now he is asking me to settle for the one piece of legislation which he promised earlier today, namely a national labour code. It is going to be good to get that, but I suggest that these other items should also be proceeded with at the earliest possible date.
We welcome the fact that there is on the order paper government order No. 39 calling for parliament to approve of the I.L.O. convention regarding discrimination in employment. We hope there will be an early opportunity for parliament to deal with that and we hope that the government will bring other I.L.O. conventions before parliament for its approval.
Because, as I say, most of what we might say we said last year, and because those things we asked for last year have not yet been implemented, and because other members wish to speak I intend to keep my remarks very brief.
There is just this other point to which I should like to give expression and it was mentioned last year after other members had spoken by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. It has been mentioned from time to time by other hon. members. I have the feeling that during the time it has taken the Liberals to implement their 1919 promises, time has moved on. Those things that would have been of tremendous advantage to the working people of Canada in the twenties, thirties, forties, and fifties, such as the national labour code that we are now perhaps going to get, are not enough to meet the conditions of our time. Automation, to which the last speaker referred, technological changes and all the changes in our economic and social structure, will make necessary far more sweeping changes than are involved

even in things like a good national labour code.
People are recognizing the fact, and economists of various schools have been speaking in this direction, that the day may soon come when we may have to provide people with an income, even though they are not engaged in what is sometimes called productive work. The whole process of automation by which we are able to produce things to make up the affluent society can change our society tremendously, and some brand new, imaginative thinking has to be done in this field. This involves more than the Department of Labour. It certainly involves the Department of Finance, it involves the whole of government policy, but the Minister of Labour is the person who should be the spokesman in the government for the great mass of our people, and in our view he should be taking the lead in any government to which he belongs to try to get some new thinking in this field. The day is going to come when, entirely apart from any productive work there may be for people to do, we are going to have to do things to expand our educational horizons; we are going to have to make it possible for people to make a contribution to our life and to our times in other ways than just trying to run machines or even pushing the buttons of an automated plant.
This is a tremendous field. I know that the minister with his academic background, is interested in it. I call upon him to bring to bear those academic thoughts that he has on the practical problem of improving the situation for the labouring people, and indeed for all the people of this country. We welcome, as I say, the improvements that are at long last in prospect, improvements promised by the Liberals 45 years ago. I suggest to the minister that if we are going to make life in Canada in the affluent sixties and seventies what it ought to be, not just for a privileged few at the top but for all the working people of the country, he still has a great deal to do. I trust he will add this as an additional supplement to the promises he has already made.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments on the matter of the
S.I.U. trustees and some of the other aspects of the estimates that have been dealt with earlier this afternoon. First of all, Mr. Chairman, I was somewhat taken aback by the exchange between the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and members on the government side with regard to the matter of Hal Banks. Much was said about it this after-
Supply-Labour
noon and it perhaps is not necessary for me to add to it, but I cannot help but think that if we were to accept that which was stated by the Leader of the Opposition in his final submission this afternoon, when he said that the administration of justice under his government in 1957 was unable to get people in this country to talk and give evidence on the crimes that had been committed and the only way that the administration some six years later could get evidence of these same crimes was through a royal commission, certainly it would be a sad commentary on the efficiency of the administration of justice under the former regime. I would be extremely surprised if the minister of justice of that time would agree with the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon.
Actually of course it was a very clever effort on the part of the Leader of the Opposition to escape what must be the decision of history that the Conservative government between 1957 and 1962 did absolutely nothing. These were the years when Hal Banks was only beginning to stretch his octopus-like tentacles across the Canadian labour movement. During those years between 1957 and 1962-
Oh, oh.
Has the hon. member got a pain? During those years between 1957 and 1962-
I sure have.

-he extended and expanded his grasp of the labour movement. During those years, the troubles on the great lakes grew. I cannot help but admire the sheer audacity of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. I am somewhat reminded of the statement that all "gall" is divided into three parts, and he has all three parts. He has the unmitigated gall to come in here and, despite the fact no action was taken against Hal Banks and the S.I.U. gangsters during his regime because the administration of justice was inefficient, say that we should have done something about Hal Banks.
Members of the opposition had been urging the Liberal government for years to take action.

It finally came to the point where only a royal commission could get the evidence needed. Yet, in spite of this the Leader of the Opposition does not avoid the point. He has the gall to come in here, change the facts around and try to say that it has

Supply-Labour
been the Liberals who have protected Banks over the years. I am sure that if the government finds Mr. Banks they will make every effort to extradite him, bring him back to Canada and face a trial. So far as I am concerned, personally, I am not sure I am in favour of that. So far as I am concerned, far more important than Hal Banks or all the Hal Bankses, is the re-establishment of peace on the great lakes. This has been accomplished through the efficiency of our present Minister of Labour. Then, I should like to see a democratic system established in the S.I.U. so that that union could be brought back into the main stream of the Canadian trade union movement.
There has been some criticism here today, somewhat disturbing criticism, of the actions of the trustees. I hope that criticism is not accurate. I hope that some time this fall the Minister of Labour will be able to prevail upon the trustees to appear before the industrial relations committee so that we may have an opportunity of discussing with the trustees what their actions have been. Until the contrary is shown to me, I am inclined to believe the trustees have been doing an effective job and that they are making progress towards the objectives that we set for them. Let us remember that hon. members who sit in the group directly opposite my very back bench-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
-were the ones who urged the setting up of this board of trustees.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. Would the hon. member who has the floor permit a question?
It would be an exquisite pleasure.
Will the hon. member agree with the Minister of Labour that Mr. Millard is doing an effective job when he claims he has not even read the Norris report?

I am not aware whether Mr. Millard has read the Norris report or not, but I am not at all convinced that is essential to doing an effective job in his position.
I believe that the trustees were set up to run the union, to return it to a democratic type of system, and to see to it we had peace on the great lakes.
I was starting out to say, and I think this pertains to the question asked by the hon. member, that members of the group directly opposite me were among those who

urged at the time that the trustees be given a free hand once the board was established to run the union, so that parliament would not be attempting to be the board of trustees itself. Actually Mr. Millard, who I presume is quite acceptable to that group because he was once an N.D.P. candidate, and the other trustees, have shown successful results. We have seen the fact that we do have peace, that commerce is moving between Canada and the United States across the great lakes.
At any price.

I am not going into the subject of how much I as a Haligonian am in favour of great lakes commerce, particularly in wintertime; but coming back to the point, the trustees should not be subjected to slighting remarks because of little differences between what they have done and what individual hon. members, 265 of them, feel that they should do. Obviously every step they take is not going to meet with the approval of everyone in this chamber; but what they have done is (a) brought peace on the lakes and (b) have brought about the position that elections are coming up in the S.I.U. in which, for the first time in many years, there will be the opportunity for the rank and file members of the S.I.U. to campaign effectively for office. We can take note of the fact that there is going to be a three cornered contest for the presidency, and contests for other positions, and I do not know what more the trustees could do than what they have done towards moving to return the S.I.U. to the rank and file of the workers and to the mainstream of Canadian democratic unionism.
I certainly deplore the fact that in some corners of this chamber every effort is made to suggest that either the trustees or the government are anxious to defend Harold Banks. Such has not been the case and I hope when the trustees do appear before a committee of the house there will be ample opportunity for this to be displayed.
Before taking my seat I wish to mention one or two other matters. I noted with interest the minister's report on the older workers' program, and I have to agree with him that it has at least reasonable success, judging from the number of older workers who had been unemployed for six to eight months prior to their applications and who have received benefits and employment. However, I think the minister and the committee would be quick to agree in this era of automation that this is only a beginning

exercise in assisting older workers, but it is a good beginning. The department should and must examine other ways by which the older worker, who becomes redundant or whose job disappears because of automation or technological changes, can make a worthwhile contribution to our economic processes and support himself and his family.
We look forward with interest to the forthcoming introduction of the national labour code, but beyond the introduction of that I would remind the minister that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act itself is badly in need of overhaul because many of its sections are out of date with conditions as they exist in industry today, and I trust the time is rapidly approaching when it will be possible to give that act a complete overhaul.

I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) who mentioned that he hoped the trustees would be appearing soon before a committee of the house. I think hon. members on all sides have expressed strong enough feelings to justify the trustees or the board chairman appearing before a committee, so that members may understand the facts. We want to know what price has been paid for the achievements of the board, as recited by the hon. member.
We know the price we paid under a Liberal administration for ridding the lakes of so-called communists. They involved us with gangsters and we are not out of that yet. We still have McLaughlin in the seats of the mighty, and therefore it is imperative that the trustees appear as soon as possible before a committee of the house. Will the minister tell the committee very definitely when arrangements are going to be made for the trustees, or the chairman, to appear before a committee of the house to give the facts about the
S.I.U., Banks and the situation on the great lakes?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.
Is the minister not going to give an answer to that very direct question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I suggest for the sake of good order in the work of the committee that we have contributions from hon. members, and the minister may answer questions later.

Mr. Chairman, other speakers have referred to the winter works program,
Supply-Labour
but not quite along the lines on which I want to discuss it briefly. I think it important to bring certain points to the direct attention of the minister before he formulates his winter works program for this year.
I believe the minister has received a brief from the Regina housebuilders association, which has a membership of 96 firms. I represent part of Regina and I am associated with the hon. member for Regina City in outlining the main points in the brief, and the points which I shall bring out also apply to my home city of Moose Jaw, and other Saskatchewan and prairie cities.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred to the defects in last winter's $500 house bonus program, and these defects are certainly apparent on the prairies. To support that assertion I will quote portions of the brief from the Regina housebuilders association. I believe the minister has received it and I imagine he has answered it, but I would like to put a few points on record. It says:
This brief from the Regina housebuilders association with a membership of 96 firms, is requesting certain changes in the $500 house bonus program of the federal government's winter works scheme.
Before proceeding to discuss the brief from the Regina housebuilders association I should like to point out that they are not opposed to a winter works incentive program but merely to the federal government's house bonus program in its present form. Members of the association feel the success or failure of this year's winter works program in their region is dependant upon certain necessary changes being made in the regulations. The brief stresses two points. One is the short period of winter employment support offered in 1963-64, namely, from December 1 to March 31. This would compare with the winter works program of the former government which started on October 15 and ended April 30. The second point they bring out is that winter building costs on the prairies greatly affect the success or failure of a winter works program. In this regard I should like to quote from the brief as follows:
Members of the Regina housebuilders association maintain that winter building costs greatly affect the success or failure of a winter works program. A national housebuilders survey of winter building costs across Canada established extra cost for winter building at from $300 to $1,100 depending on the region in Canada in which the house is built. This means builders in areas that have an average extra winter building cost of $300 have a $200 incentive to offer their purchasers if they buy a winter built house.. .but builders in areas where climatic conditions are very

Supply-Labour
severe, such as those in the prairie region, have nothing to offer except costs in excess of the bonus amount.
A further point made in the brief is this:
In addition, winter works houses this year will have to bear the increase of most of the cost of the 3 per cent sales tax increase to go into effect January 1, 1965.
They are referring to the fact that on January 1 there will be a federal sales tax of 11 per cent on building materials. The recommendation in the brief on this particular point is:
The Regina housebuilders association, therefore, respectfully requests the Department of Labour to increase the amount of the winter works bonus paid the purchaser by an amount equal to the difference between winter costs in the most favourable region of Canada and those found in the region in which the house is being built.
I think this is a reasonable recommendation to place before the minister and I hope it will be given consideration. The brief goes on:
Regina housebuilders realize the federal government's winter works bonus plan has been designed to stimulate construction and create employment during the winter months when unemployment is usually at a peak. They also acknowledge that the 1963-64 winter works program was designed to alleviate this condition by promoting employment between December 1 and March 31 each winter.
However, unemployment in the prairie region occurs earlier in the fall and remains later in the spring than in other areas of Canada.
The recommendation made to the minister is as follows:
We therefore respectfully request the federal Department of Labour to consider the merits of extending the winter works $500 house bonus program to include the spring and fall periods of unemployment in the prairie regions.. .especially November and April.
As I mentioned before, the program of the last government began on October 15 and ended on April 30.
Another point brought out in the brief is this:
Regina housebuilders wish to point out that during the 1963-64 winter works bonus program, the Department of Labour refused to recognize an irrevocable assignment or power of attorney from the purchaser, thus enabling the builder to collect the $500 bonus amount from the government as part of the purchaser's house payment. Builders maintained they were entitled to payment for a completed product before occupancy and refused occupancy until payment was forthcoming. Consequently, many purchasers, and especially those in the lower income groups, were unable to raise the required amount and were forced by this requirement to find other accommodation at additional expense until their bonus application was processed by the government.
The recommendation in this respect is as follows:
The association therefore, respectfully requests the Department of Labour to recognize a standard irrevocable assignment by the purchaser of the $500 bonus amount.
Again I would point out that though this is a brief presented by the Regina housebuilders association, in bringing it forward I am speaking also for other builders in Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and the prairies generally. The brief, at its conclusion, makes the following request:
Members of the Regina housebuilders association would strongly urge the federal Department of Labour to give immediate consideration to the recommendations for change as outlined in this brief so that they may be implemented before the 1964-65 winter works house bonus program goes into effect this fall.
I trust the minister will carefully consider these recommendations and incorporate them in the winter works program.

I am inclined to agree, if I may say this on entering the discussion, with the comments made by my colleague about the minister's charm. It would appear to me that after the first flush of success which the minister enjoyed he has, in the last year, somewhat faded away. The only thing I have discovered about him in the last six or seven months is that he does not know much about baseball, compared with the Prime Minister. I do not suppose that is a serious handicap.
Some of us regret that he did not accept the position offered him as leader of the house. In view of the fact that he has been able to bring forward little of his legislative program and that he has not been embroiled in any great labour difficulty such as arises from time to time in connection with the railroads, I might comment that the hon. gentleman might well have accepted that position. If he had done so, maybe, with his charm, we would have been further along with our work this session.
I have one concrete proposal to put to the minister. It is at least current in that it ties in with the discussion going on in the country with regard to the appointment of an ombudsman fired by the visit of Sir Guy Powles of New Zealand. In my experience in labour matters, and because of my work in relation to railway unions in particular, between six and a dozen cases are brought to my notice every year of grievances felt by workers, sometimes with their own unions but more often with the way their complaints have been processed and the difficulties which arise in dealing with an international union whose final decisions are taken in the United States.


I had a case brought to my attention the other day, a case from Cornwall involving a man by the name of Kuntz who was in difficulty with the hospital employees union. It was taken up through the Canadian vice president and then it went before the Ontario labour relations board. The grievance was not upheld but in my judgment, having reviewed all the files-this is not a federal matter and I am mentioning it only as an example-this man still needs assistance. This case still needs review. I myself can see, implicit in the case in which he is involved, a tremendous tendency for the agents of the union and of the employers to co-operate in snuffing out this man's complaint, because of the trouble it would cause in terms of both the unit in which the case is involved and the membership of the union.
I have another case in connection with a railway trainman on the west coast, a man by the name of Woods, who for three years has been trying to get a grievance settled. He has lost out partly by default, it seems to me, within the union processes. I have taken it up with management and they always come back to me and say there are the proper arrangements within the contract for the man to settle his grievance.
I would like to suggest that in the United States at least one union, the steelworkers, has set up an outside court. Even the S.I.U., in the last gesture, I believe, that Mr. Banks made of any substance to indicate that the
S.I.U. was a good union, created this appeal board with Commander Robertson in charge. I think there is a spirit in the labour movement, particularly in some of the more progressive unions, in the United States to say that it is a great advantage to labour if, when a particular worker has a grievance and suspects collusion between the union leadership and management, he can go to someone who is above and beyond management, government or labour-someone, in a sense, in the judicial field who has almost a judicial status and the kind of freedom to move that an ombudsman has-to settle his grievance.
Obviously, Mr. Chairman, if we are to get this kind of an officer in Canada it is going to take a great deal of co-operation in developing the idea of the office; because it needs a co-operative program perhaps on the part of 11 different departments of labour and it needs the substantial support of an organization such as the Canadian Labour Congress, and even the unions that are sometimes referred to as maverick unions that
Supply-Labour
are outside the Canadian Labour Congress. I think this is a very, very worth-while idea. Partly it is a good defensive move for the labour movement itself, and partly it appeals to me because I have become more and more concerned, in my time in politics, with the poor individual citizen who gets caught up within a bureaucracy, whether it is of management, labour or government. This is something that is of increasing difficulty. I think it is a feather in the cap of the trade union movement as I know it that so few cases do come forward; that their grievance procedure does settle so many things.
I do not think there would be a welter of these complaints. I do not think it would have any effect on the normal working of the grievance procedure. But I do suggest that the minister should consider giving the lead in trying to obtain co-operation from the provincial departments of labour and from the labour movement as a whole in setting up in Canada the kind of organization and system based upon a labour ombudsman, and having some similarity in its terms of reference to what has been created in the United States by the united steelworkers. It seems to me that if the terms of reference for such an office were properly worked out, for example so that the office did not get involved in any jurisdictional disputes, and if there was a question of jurisdictional difference that would be wiped out, this would benefit those in the labour field.
One of the most important reasons for our needing this office is that judicial recourse is so rarely useful or so rarely open to a worker with this kind of grievance. This gentleman who came to see me from Cornwall has been out of work for two years. He had difficulty getting the bus fare to come to Ottawa, let alone the money necessary to hire a lawyer. I have just enough of these cases, four or five a year, to indicate to me -and I assume that other members have had similar cases brought to their attention-that this would be a very worth-while move to consider. Perhaps we should expect the unions to develop this idea in the way that Commander Robertson has developed it within the S.I.U. But I suggest it would be an imaginative step if we had such an office for the whole country. I would like the minister to give this suggestion serious consideration. I think it would be a real contribution.
One of the points where government and bureaucracy madden me is, for example, with the little gandy dance that has gone on between the minister and the hon. member for

Supply-Labour
Danforth in connection with the unemployment insurance commission, the Toronto newspaper strike and the question as to whether the strikers, or the people who have been locked out, as they claim, should be eligible tor unemployment insurance benefits. We have this whole question of 85 per cent production. Why in the name of heavens in a case like this cannot there be a bit more dispatch? I have connections with one newspaper, and to a degree with another newspaper, at both the management and union level. It has been apparent for more than two weeks that those newspapers are in practically full production. When we hear this talk about a production of 85 per cent, we realize it is nonsense when we read the editions of the Telegram and Star. They have been putting out 76-page and 72-page editions. When you look at the amount of classified advertising, this point is brought home, because you do not get a paper of 76 pages in the city of Toronto unless you have a very large output. Having talked to the management of at least one of the papers, who say they are as efficient, if not more efficient, than they were before the strike started, I do not know how the minister can be satisfied with this kind of delay. Maybe to the bureaucrat's mind a delay of one, two or three weeks is not much; but it sure means a great deal to those strikers and the income they have, in comparison with what they seem to me to be entitled to from the unemployment insurance commission.
I certainly think the minister could, in co-operation with the head of the unemployment insurance commission, settle this matter with about three phone calls to Toronto. Maybe this is not the way you should do things; maybe you should send registered letters-I don't know. But I think three phone calls would confirm to the minister's satisfaction that there is a lot more than 85 per cent production in those newspapers.
One of the points I wanted to make in connection with the S.I.U., as I have heard the kettle addressing the pot here this afternoon in this connection as to who is responsible, is that it is very apparent from the correspondence that is filed in connection with the Norris report that the question of how the S.I.U. was behaving was brought to the attention of the former minister of labour and the previous government quite early on in its administration. I know it was brought to their attention right in this house, because I brought it to their attention, and so did the hon. member for Kootenay West. As a matter

of fact, I received a number of virulent phone calls and letters over it. I also hope that the minister has read the speech, Hal Banks' speech, made last year at the S.I.U. international convention in the United States. I think this speech is worthy of his perusal. Hal was delighted with the Canadian situation because his buddies were back; the Liberals were back in power and all the noisiness of those silly New Democrats and the stubbornness, bullheadedness and the unfairness of the Diefenbaker government had disappeared, because his pals were back.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Oh, you don't believe that.
That is what Hal Banks said.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: But you don't believe it.

He was convinced of it. I know there is an element of guilt amongst the Liberals in a Liberal administration over the relationship the party has had with the S.I.U. and Mr. Banks. I could get worked up about this personally, since the S.I.U. moved right into my own area to work with the Liberal organization in order to try and defeat me in two election campaigns. They were welcome; it was great to have them. But, Mr. Chairman, there has been an identity in the minds of a great many people between the Liberal party and Hal Banks. However, I do not want to go digging up again the whole business of how Mr. Banks and Mr. McLaughlin used to refer to Walter Harris as their Ottawa office.
I am not going to get into what I think is the kind of corn introduced by the former prime minister in connection with the recognition of red China, when he suggested that red China had to expiate its sins before Canada could give recognition. I am not suggesting that the minister or the government have to expiate any sin, but I do hope that their guilt makes them uncomfortable enough to feel that it will not be satisfactory just to do a little surface tidying up of the situation.
A few weeks ago I had the pleasure of going through the Welland canal on a freighter, calling at a United States port and then going on to the lakehead. I talked to the sailors and several of the men who were witnesses before the Norris commission. They all welcomed the fact that there is peace on the lakes. But not even the simplest among them is under any illusion that the situation has been cleared up or that it is permanently remedied. They do not expect the bombs to start bursting this year but they do expect it

next year. They say it is useless to think that the tactics of the S.I.U. which have been built up over a generation in the United States are suddenly going to disappear. There will probably be peace as long as we have a trusteeship, and then the battle will develop again.
It seems to me that the only alternative is for the trusteeship really to develop a democratic approach. I took a gentleman in to see the minister a week ago. This man had been fired off a ship at the lakehead. This was despite the fact that he had an excellent record and had been with that ship for a couple of years. He also had a letter from the vice president of the C.S.L. recommending him for further training for a master's ticket. He had been fired off his ship without warning by an officer of the ship, who actually was not responsible for him, and on a phony excuse -at least, according to Mr. Mallett. But the interesting thing is Mr. Mallett's position in the union. He was against the march to Ottawa last year. He had stood, with a certain amount of bravery in my mind, against the size of the union fee membership and against any special levies. He had also been told by two officials of the S.I.U.: "You just wait, mister". Well, they got him and he now is involved in a court case, which comes under the Canada Shipping Act and which I will not comment on. I think they have got him, but many difficulties have since ensued. Now, here is a man fired off a ship. There is a grievance procedure, but has it worked well? I would say it has not, because to my mind there has been collusion to a degree between management and union officials in order to get rid of an objectionable character. That is my personal opinion.
My point is that this kind of situation does not occur in a good union. You are not going to get an arbitrary firing of a man who has an excellent record just overnight for a very minor excuse. I am just dismayed at the prospect of peace so long as the trustees are there, with the trustees not carrying out a thorough enough reform to make sure that it becomes a democratic organization. I realize we have to suspend judgment for a little longer, but I have a hunch that despite the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) the minister and his officials are no more enamoured with some of the things which have developed in this situation than I am. I would hope that the minister has a breaking point, and that that breaking point will be when he becomes convinced that real reform is not taking place. I trust that he will then let us know, and that any guilt
Supply-Labour
complex which may exist will reinforce my contention that he should let us know. We will look forward to hearing the trustees before the committee.
I want to switch now to a matter which has been a very great disappointment both to myself and to a number of other members of the house, particularly to a number of Conservative members who represent railway points. I think of the late Sherwood Rideout and of all the work he did for the railway workers. It is a fact that last year the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines had before it the subject matter of a bill which I brought in. That committee almost unanimously-there was one exception-after long hearings listening to the vice presidents of both railways and hearing labour representatives, led off by the senior citizen of Canadian railway labour, Frank Hall, brought in recommendations in connection with the Railway Act. But we have in the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-that Manitoba carpetbagger who got into Newfoundland and took charge of the department-a very skilful person at sitting on something so that all you get is inaction, inertia, and finally disappearance.
I put it to the minister that amongst the railway workers this issue has not disappeared, despite the fact that contracts have been signed. I also put it to the minister that the Minister of Transport promised when Donald Gordon was before the committee some time ago that as these recommendations which we made in connection with dislocation costs and the effects of automation and technical changes on the railways was so large an issue it should properly fall within the scope of the Department of Labour. That is what he said and I think there is a certain amount of reasonableness to it. Then he was prodded about this and said yes, he thought the Minister of Labour would be interested and that it should be within that framework. But we have not heard a damned thing about it since. It seems to me that it is almost typical of the slowness with which this administration works.
The minister knows, despite the big glossy title of Minister of Labour for Canada, that the main group of workers who come under his jurisdiction are the railway workers of Canada. I think he would acknowledge that the great bulk of his routine work in labour relations matters is connected with the railroad. I am surprised that the minister and his officials have had so little interest in the recommendations of that committee. Those

Supply-Labour
recommendations were made by a committee of this parliament on which members of the party to which he belongs took quite an active part. I would suggest to him that one of the answers we would like at this time in discussing his estimates is what he is going to do about this matter. I can be quite specific about it. If he wants to check the evidence given by the Minister of Transport before the special committee which heard Donald Gordon, he will find it all in the report, and in several places the Minister of Transport made statements which I had certainly assumed would lead to some kind of communication with the government, so that the minister would have some answer.
Another question I want to put to the minister is this. I, and I think a lot of other hon. members, would like an assessment of the vocational and technical school building program into which the federal government has poured so many millions of dollars. I was staggered when I saw that the Ontario minister of education is going to throw up another $4 million structure for retraining purposes somewhere soon. Wherever I go across the province I run into these big piles of schools which have come out of recent programs. For example, in the lakehead we have a number of them. We have some very good programs going on, but a great many people-educators, teachers, even the unemployed and the people in the unemployment insurance commission and national employment service-are not convinced that we are providing the right kind of facilities or offering the right kind of courses.
We have had an excellent crop of buildings, but in view of the fact that the federal government has put hundreds of millions of dollars into this program I think it is about time that we had some kind of assessment from the government of what has followed from all this building. I want to repeat one of my suspicions in connection with this matter. I think many of the provinces have got good, new secondary school plants out of the program but I am not so sure we have really created enough space of the right kind for a real retraining program. I think we need an assessment.
One of the reasons why I ask the minister for this is that I have great respect for the work of Mr. Ford of his department, although I do not know him personally. I have read enough of the contributions to the written record that Mr. Ford has made at various times to sense that he has been concerned and somewhat disturbed about this huge pro-

gram which is moving along on an ad hoc basis. I think we should have an appreciation
as to how successful this big spending program has been in terms of concrete results leading to work.
The last point I want to make to the minister relates to the publications of his department dealing with automation. I have just seen the first occasional paper by a Mr. McDonald in connection with office automation. I thought it standard was much higher than most I have seen from the department. It was much higher in the sense that it was both readable and yet had enough substance to it that you had something more than just the big bulky mimeographed reports that we used to get from the department in connection with matters like this and which always seemed to be a welter of statistics. I should like to suggest that the department should be encouraged to produce more papers like this and to give them wide distribution and as much publicity as possible. I certainly know that out of that one paper I can get a great deal of material to answer workers in offices in all kinds of industries. I should like to compliment the department on this particular publication and I hope there will be more of them. There are all kinds of things one can raise on this issue.
I suppose I should pay a compliment to the minister on two things, since they deal with his officials. In the last few months I have noticed a remarkable dropping off in individual complaints about the unemployment insurance commission and its officials. Part of that may be due to good times but I think a part of it is the result of the fact that things have finally settled down to an even keel after the adjustment that took place as a result of the tightening of the regulations a year or two ago. From my experience I think the commission should be complimented on this.
The other point on which I should like to compliment the minister also relates to the work of the unemployment insurance commission. If I can judge by my own area and by what I see in the newspapers of other areas the unemployment insurance commission is having much more success in the last while in moving in a public relations way to lead people to see that the commission is more than just a routine organization and that they tie in closely with the national employment service and with educational institutions and job opportunities. I may be wrong in sensing this improvement, but I certainly see it in my own area.

There are other matters in relation to the Department of Labour that I might mention to the minister. Really he has the same challenge as the Minister of Forestry in trying to develop joint programs. His department is really enmeshed in joint programs, particularly with regard to anything concerning education. I think that some day some educator in this country who has political responsibility, and the minister is an educator, is going to have the courage to get up and say: Joint programs are all very well but they are massive, they are slow and they are complicated. This minister is going to ask for more federal authority in this field, particularly with regard to retraining. He is going to ask for the surrender by the provinces of some of their privileges in this particular educational area. I should like to think that the present minister would be the one who would consider doing that.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take part in the discussion this afternoon but after listening to the remarks of the last speaker with regard to the strike in Toronto involving the three daily newspapers I feel I must rise. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for being truthful and honest in calling the episode now in progress in Toronto a strike. It is a strike. There was an endeavour to call it a lockout, but an injunction was secured in the supreme court of Ontario prohibiting the use of that term because it is a strike and not a lockout.
I should like to congratulate the Department of Labour and the minister for the manner in which they are handling the unemployment insurance fund in this specific case. We would all be howling to high heaven if the federal government in any manner, shape or form should appear to be acting as a strikebreaker in a strike, and I am sure we would also complain if the federal government should in any way appear to be financing a strike. I have no quarrel with the manner in which the Department of Labour is handling the unemployment insurance fund with regard to this situation in Toronto. These men all had good positions and were well paid, and paid regularly. They chose to strike of their own volition. It is no function of the unemployment insurance fund to finance them if they now find the going a little tough, after having made this decision themselves.
I should almost like to ask the question whether the last speaker was showing some self-interest in this matter. The strikers were somewhat riled over his crossing the picket
Supply-Labour
lines, and any request to the Minister of Labour to release money to these strikers may be with the idea that this money will assuage their feelings toward a man who crossed the picket lines. I should like to congratulate the Minister of Labour on the way in which he is handling this matter and to tell him not to be in too much of a hurry to meet the request of the last speaker on this point.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be just as brief as the hon. member who spoke before me.
As one who represents an essentially rural constituency, I should just like to say that I would be most happy if farm labourers came under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Our farmers are looking for cheap labour. They are often accused of mechanizing their farms, but if relatively cheap labour were available, they would undoubtedly take advantage of it.
Most often, such labour is not available because farm hands are not covered by unemployment insurance. I have taken every opportunity to bring this discrepancy to the attention of the authorities and once again I should like to advocate that farm labourers be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take only a few moments to make certain remarks to the minister. I know he is anxious to conclude the debate. I know he has promised the committee to give them certain specific pieces of information and I am sure he is anxious to get his estimates through. I want to bring to his attention a situation I have mentioned before in the house. My experience of the twenty sixth parliament is that sometimes you have to say something many, many times before it even registers either with the ministers or with their officials.
I am particularly pleased to see the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the house at this time because the suggestion I want to make to the Minister of Labour is a constructive one and almost involves a joint endeavour. The house is probably aware that there is absolutely no labour legislation whatsoever in the Northwest Territories. I think it is unfortunate that in 1964, when we are approaching the celebration of our 100th birthday, there should be a part of Canada where there is no protection whatsoever for the working man.

Supply-Labour
There are no laws guaranteeing minimum wages. There are no laws concerning hours of work, paid holidays, overtime pay or any of these things. I know, before the minister or anyone else tells me, that it is essentially a matter for the territorial council to provide legislation on these subjects. This is really where the minister of northern affairs comes in. At this particular juncture the minister of northern affairs has the peculiar responsibility of giving leadership to the council to see that this kind of legisation is prepared, in co-operation with the Minister of Labour, and presented to the territorial council. The fact of the matter is that the bulk of the councillors on that council are appointed by the cabinet, so there is an extra measure of federal control.
I say it is a serious problem because when we are talking about unemployment in Canada and the efforts the various administrations have made and are making to combat it, I think it is worth observing that in some of the more northerly areas of Canada at certain times of the year the unemployment rate is in fact 100 per cent. Now, this may not involve very many people in terms of the Canadian population. However, I suggest to you that it involves parts of the country that have a total population of approximately 100,000. I am thinking of the northerly parts of the provinces and, in particular, of the two northern territories. At times, the people who live in those parts of the country have absolutely no means of obtaining employment. These people are nearly all Indian or Eskimo people who have, over the course of the past few years, lost not only their initiative in connection with trapping, hunting and fishing, but in many cases have lost the skills necessary to conduct those activities properly.
I was pleased at the statement issued yesterday by the minister of northern affairs as a result of another northern tour which he has just completed, and a most successful one. This statement referred to the educational programs which are so desperately needed and which will have a long term effect on the life of the northern people. All that we have succeeded in doing so far is taking the Indian and Eskimo children and moving them out of their own way of life into a no man's land. I know of several communities in the Northwest Territories and the northern parts of the provinces where at times of the year when hunting, fishing and fur trapping are not profitable, the entire community may be out of work. When the minister is giving a statement on unemployment in Canada, it

must be a source of irritation to him that there are still these pockets in our country where unemployment may reach as high as 90 per cent for a few months in the year.
I want to make a suggestion to the minister. I was interested in his opening remarks about the economic research branch and the kind of analyses the branch is doing or is planning to do. I want to suggest to him that it would be worth while if he asked this branch to conduct a survey of the unemployment situation in Canada's northerly regions. I mean a real survey and not something that is done in a week or ten days. The minister should give this branch the task of finding out what the situation really is; what skills there are in the groups of people who are, as I suggested earlier, Indian and Eskimo people. He should ascertain methods by which they can be brought back into the employment stream. I suggest the Department of Labour do this, rather than the department of northern affairs, because the federal department of northern affairs is already involved in providing an ameliorating program, if you can call it that. I refer to the educational facilities, and so on.
Quite often when a federal department like northern affairs is so intimately involved in the administration of an area their survey would tend to be an apology for what they have been doing or have not been doing. Quite often the officials of a department, particularly northern affairs, will say that everything is fine and the programs they have been conducting are wonderful; there are no other methods that could be followed. I ask the Minister of Labour to conduct this survey through the economic research branch. This is a specific task and it may take some months. Certainly, from his description of the branch it would be the ideal organization to undertake this work. They would be really rendering a service to northern Canadians wherever they may be found, not only in the territories but also in the provinces.
I want to make a suggestion to him. I should like the department to look into the possibility of the government of Canada, which is the largest single employer in the Canadian north, making more use of local labour. The record of the government of Canada over the years in employing local people has not been good. Quite often, and I speak on the basis of experience in the Canadian north as a federal employee, we were pressuring private enterprise, construction companies that came in to work on projects and so on, to give work to the Indian

and Eskimo people. We said, you should not be importing thousands of labourers from the south when we have all these people here. However the record of the government itself has not been good. For this reason I suggest the Department of Labour, because it represents the only federal department that is not in the Northwest Territories in a major way. They have nothing to protect, not even any empire to preserve. I use those words advisedly. I think they would have to take action with objectivity, with a special perspective that would allow the officials of this department to do the work. I urgently request the minister to consider this.
There is just one other thing I want to request the minister to do, and that is to establish at least one office for the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service in the northern territories. At the present time if a person wishes to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits or even attempt to find work in other parts of the country, the nearest office is Edmonton which is some 500 miles south of our southerly border. If you live over in the eastern part of the territories you have to contact Montreal. I have placed a question on the order paper before about this and received an answer from the minister's officials that there is no need for the Department of Labour to establish either an employment office or an unemployment insurance office in the Northwest Territories; everything is fine; the officials are watching things and it is under constant survey.
The bitter truth in relation to this situation was revealed when one of the producing gold mines in Yellowknife shut down last winter and some 150 men were put out of work for a few months. The unemployment insurance office did not even have enough forms in Edmonton to handle the situation. I suggest to the minister that the volume of business in the Canadian Northwest Territories justifies a full scale office and it would be advisable to have one set up. I can guarantee him that business will be booming, if he does in fact provide facilities. Right now people just have to depend on neighbours or friends to do this. It is not as good as the service that is being provided by the unemployment insurance commission in many, many regions. Many residents who are eligible for benefits simply do not know about it and consequently use other facilities offered through the department of northern affairs, such as the public welfare program and relief,
Supply-Labour
when in fact they could be benefiting from the placement service.
Before taking my seat to allow the minister to make his concluding comments, I want to bring his attention to the situation on the distant early warning line. He promised me previously that he would look into it. The situation is one which has been going on for some years and I would like him to indicate now, or later to me privately, whether his department is looking into the complaint that American employees of the Federal Electric Corporation receive substantially more pay than Canadian employees doing the same work. I have had this complaint for some months now. I was dimly aware of it when I worked along the distant early warning line, but more recently it has been brought forcibly to my attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
My intervention in this debate will be short and is caused only by the fact the previous speaker referred to labour conditions in the territories. I want to assure him we have been aware of the complaints that have been registered in respect of the letting of contracts in Edmonton, with no requirement in the territories covering the normal rates of pay that exist in Edmonton. There has also been a complaint in respect to the workmen's compensation in the territories, on the basis of inadequacy.
We are not unaware of this, and I would hope the hon. member would give us some marks for the fact that we have forthrightly attempted to take care of these matters in the appointment within our power of at least one member of the Northwest Territories council. We have appointed to that council Mr. Stuart Hodgson, who is an extremely well known and highly regarded member of the international woodworkers of America.
I have asked him to act in respect of these matters as a labour man might be expected to act, and nothing more. I know he called the labour council in the city of Edmonton to meet them. They gave him an entire day and I have reports from them that they were exceedingly well pleased for what they described as the first time a government had attempted to meet them in respect of these matters.
My hon. friend is aware of the difficulties in respect of using and incorporating the indigenous people in the work force there. I think we have made pretty fair progress and I believe he thinks so too. At one time we had 100 Eskimos working in a mine in the territories and they turned out to be extremely adept in using machinery, and

Supply-Labour
competent of adopting new techniques. Unfortunately the mine ran out of ore, but we transferred a number of them to other mines. There are now 10 Eskimo families working at Yellowknife, respected and accepted by the white community, and doing a very splendid job for the firms employing them. These are conditions towards which we are moving, and we will do our best in co-operation with the Northwest Territories council to take care of these matters brought before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I think I hear the Secretary of State murmur a bit because he sees me rise, but I can tell him right away I am going to have my say because I promised a number of people in B.C. that I would make a few remarks on the estimates of the Department of Labour.
Excuse me, I did not.

Then I apologize. I must have had a poor ear. This is a most inspiring atmosphere in which to deal with labour matters; I can see the committee is in a very cheerful and agreeable mood. I wish to say I listened to the minister's opening statement with interest and appreciation, as he outlined certain policies and programs of the department. I am not going to deal with those, except to say that I for one am very pleased to see willingness to experiment. I am not one who would criticize if an experiment fails. In this field the idea of experimenting is well worth while. We are entering into a new era so far as labour relations, automation and so on are concerned, and I am sure the only way to find sound solutions is as a result of experimentation from time to time. I am very glad to see these experiments being carried on with respect to legislation programs, and administration.
I have a few remarks to make on other matters which concern a number of workers. I am one of those persons who keep in touch with the rank and file of the workers organizations and unions because I have always found that if I keep close to the rank and file of labour, the farmers, and people in general, I have nothing to fear regardless of what anybody else says.
I have a few comments to make in respect to the maritime trustees and the famous Hal Banks binge, as I was possibly the first member to raise the question in the house of his activities, his past record and so on. As a result of that I aroused his ire, and he sent one of his colleagues around my constituency circulating literature wherever he
[Mr. Laing.l
could find an opportunity to distribute it, in stores, Legion branches, clubs and trade union offices, condemning me as a proper bounder. Anyway I was very pleased because once people read his opinion of me their regard for me was higher than it was previously. That was before the 1957 election.
I support the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur in respect to this question. We in this group have some concern as to the ultimate conclusion of the operations of the maritime union trustees. I am not underestimating their difficulties. Some members have been critical of the former government with respect to this situation, but at least a royal commission was appointed by that government, a commission that finally brought out the facts and caused some action to be taken.
