On numerous occasions during 1956 and the early part of 1957 hon. members of the opposition rose in the house and urged the Liberal government to take some action with respect to this man. I repeatedly urged that he be deported and, regardless of the situation now, let us not forget that this man was brought to Canada as a result of action of the Liberal government in which I consider there was monkey-work with the immigration papers when he arrived, which concealed his former criminal record.
There should be an early appearance of the maritime trustees before the industrial relations committee because I remember that on April 4, Mr. Charles Millard, one of the trustees, issued a joint statement with Mr. Paul Hall, president of the S.I.U. of North America, announcing they had reached agreement. Their peace formula included the following, and I quote:
The vice president of the S.I.U., Leonard McLaughlin, would take over as president of the
5.1.	U.
Active management of the S.I.U. would be turned back to S.I.U. leaders.
The Canadian S.I.U. will continue as part of the
5.1.	U. of North America.
Maritime unions on the great lakes will be integrated.
Later it was stated that integration meant that the two Canadian unions on the great lakes-the Canadian maritime union and the seamen's section of the Canadian brotherhood of railway and transport workers-would be taken over by the
5.1.	U.
That peace formula has not developed, but it indicates Mr. Millard's line of thought and I for one object very strongly to any action to permit the S.I.U. to take over these unions which fought the good fight against Hal Banks and his S.I.U. associates when the going was very difficult. These Canadian

unions did a great deal to bring the matter to a head, focus public attention upon it and, ultimately, bring about action by the government.
I think the trustees should appear before a committee of this house and give us some idea of their objectives and their methods, as well as some understanding of what they have achieved to date. I am not understimat-ing the difficulties. I think everyone wants to see this question resolved satisfactorily and for all time. I hope the committee members will have the opportunity to question the trustees-not just the chairman, but all of the trustees. Some of us would like to put certain questions to them individually, and I hope the minister will make this possible at an early date.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I have mentioned it before in the house and I repeat it at the request of union members concerned with the British Columbia hydro power authority legislation. Members of the unions directly concerned are anxious about this, as is the trade union movement generally in British Columbia. In 1954, Premier Duplessis had an amendment made to the Quebec labour legislation making it illegal for all unions connected with public services to strike. That law was in effect until recent times. Owing to the strong position taken by Quebec trade unions-and I give them full credit for it-Premier Lesage has agreed to amend this act and delete those vicious clauses so that employees of public services will have the right to strike; they will have this freedom returned to them. Only the firefighters and the police are excepted.
Just the reverse is happening in British Columbia. At the last session of the legislature, amendments were made to the hydro and power authority act making it illegal for employees of the hydro authority to strike. In case the minister has not noticed this, I refer to subsection (2) of section 56 of the act which passed third reading in the legislature of British Columbia on March 10, 1964. It reads as follows;
No person shall declare or authorize a strike, and no employee of the authority shall strike, and the authority shall not lock out any employee or employees.
I have mentioned this before and brought it to the attention of the Minister of Justice. I mentioned it again at the request of many of the employees concerned. They are disturbed about it and I cannot understand the authority supporting this legislation. This is
Supply-Labour
a type of organization within which strikes are most infrequent and I cannot understand them damaging public relations with their employees by having this provision included in the hydro and power authority act. I urge the minister to discuss this matter with the Minister of Justice because, like a good many other people, I think there are sound grounds for the disallowance of this legislation as a transgression of the Canadian Bill of Rights. The federal government has the right to disallow legislation if there is sound reason for doing so. I bring this to the attention of the minister because I know that at heart he is a small "1" liberal who is very conscious of this aspect of our social fabric. I know many trade unions in British Columbia would welcome an assurance that this legislation will be disallowed.
Now I wish to deal with another question for a few minutes. I do so at the request of trade unionists because of the coming developments on the Columbia in the course of which large contracts will be let. Undoubtedly a good many of these contracts will go to corporations controlled in the United States, because many of these companies have the type of equipment required and are able to underbid Canadian firms. I mention this because we had one experience during the construction of the pipe line in British Columbia which brings it to mind. I speak particularly of southeastern British Columbia where I know what happened from personal experience. Hundreds of United States workers crossed the line into Canada as landed immigrants. I am not blaming them for seeking employment. Of course they had to indicate that they intended to settle in Canada. On the whole, these were completely false declarations. They came to Canada and worked on these pipe line jobs for periods of between three months and six months to my knowledge. In order to find out whether or not these people were landed immigrants, the R.C.M.P. checked their cards, and practically all of them had visitors' permits saying they intended to return to the United States within a few months. These men obtained employment from United States controlled construction companies while Canadian workers in the area were unemployed. Students at the university of British Columbia who were looking forward to making a little extra money in the summer months were denied the opportunity to do so because of the number of United States citizens who had come in as landed immigrants to take employment in connection with the construe-

Supply-Labour
tion of the pipe line and who then, with very few exceptions, returned to the United States.
The second thing I wish to complain of is this. These companies completely ignored the national employment service. I talked to the manager of the employment service at Nelson at that time and he told me that the manager of one of these companies had said: We are not going to be bothered with your petty national employment service; we shall employ whom we wish and in the way we wish. I thought this was a high handed way to treat our national employment service. The office there had a list of local people for 200 miles around who were anxious to get employment on these projects. I bring this up because, as I said before, numerous United States controlled companies will undoubtedly get contracts in connection with the Columbia development project and I suggest to the minister that some consideration be given to amending the Immigration Act or to tightening up the regulations or to checking more closely so as to make certain that those who apply to come to Canada as landed immigrants really intend to settle in Canada. I fully agree there must be reciprocity on this question. We have Canadians who wish to enter the United States to take up employment, not so much from western Canada as from the eastern areas. But I do think something could be done to amend the act or the regulations and strengthen the hands of the officials at the ports of entry so that they can check this practice. The British Columbia hydro and power authority has indicated that it would employ persons who have been in Canada for 60 days. Well, it is easy to come to Canada for a couple of months to await the commencement of a four or five year program. I suggest the department should do something to see that the services of the national employment service are used by these organizations. I think it is highly improper that the national facilities should be ignored to the disadvantage of Canadian citizens. I would also suggest that it would be a good idea for the Department of Labour to have occasional observers at these large construction projects to find out how the law and the regulations are being complied with, to see how the national employment service is being used, and for the government to get well informed, from a national angle, as to the application of labour law and regulations to the advantage of Canadian citizens.
I had intended to speak for another ten or 15 minutes, Mr. Chairman; but I will leave my further remarks to another occasion

in order to give the minister an opportunity to reply at this time if he wishes to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member who has just resumed his seat for his consideration in shortening his remarks so I might have a chance to make some comments on a number of points that have been raised by hon. gentlemen in the discussion this afternoon. I certainly thank hon. members for the searching examination they have given the work of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission. I especially wish to thank them for the well merited commendations they have paid to members of my department and the unemployment insurance commission. I have already stated that it is the intention of the government to introduce comprehensive labour standards legislation at this session, and it is my firm expectation that it will be placed on the order paper in the month of September. Criminal Code
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is a very simple one. Most people in Canada, particularly people who are interested in labour-management relations, have assumed for some considerable time that the law of the country provided for the right of workers who wished to join unions of their choice to do so without discrimination against them and without difficulties being put in their way. The Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act makes this position very clear. Section 3, subsection 1 reads as follows:
Every employee has the right to be a member of a trade union and to participate in the activities thereof.
This right has not been challenged too often in Canada. Certainly it has not been challenged in most of the cities of Canada. It has not been too difficult for trade union organizers and rank and file members of trade unions interested in getting workers in their industry to join their union, to visit people in their homes or in public places in order to make clear to them the reasons why they should join and to give them the legitimate right to join.
Difficulties have arisen in recent years as resources of Canada in previously inaccessible areas have been developed. Problems have arisen in the mining industry, in the building of hydroelectric plants and in the lumbering industry, to mention just a few. What employers who have desired to get around the provision in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which I have just quoted, have done is to use a provision in the Criminal Code, which in my opinion was never meant to be used when it was drafted for the purpose of preventing union organizers from having the opportunity to speak to people on the job. Section 41, subsection 1, of the Criminal Code, which deals with defence of house or real property, reads as follows:
Every one who is in peaceable possession of a dwelling house or real property and every one lawfully assisting him or acting under his authority is justified in using force to prevent any person from trespassing on the dwelling house or real property, or to remove a trespasser therefrom, if he uses no more force than is necessary.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the inaccessible areas of Canada when mining operations or lumber operations are opened up the companies have to build bunkhouses for the workers, since there is no other place for them to live. In my opinion the workers who live there have the same rights to have visitors as any other people living in a city or town in a house or an apartment building. This is the place where they live. In my opinion they have a right, and

they ought to have a right, to have the same kind of visitors as freely and as easily as people living in the cities or towns of Canada. That has not happened. It is for this reason I have proposed in this bill to add subsection 3 to section 41 of the Criminal Code, which would read as follows:
Except where a landlord would be therein justified under a covenant with a tenant for quiet enjoyment, nothing in this section shall be deemed to justify an employer in using force to prevent any person from having ingress to, regress over, or egress from a dwelling house or real property in or upon which the employer houses an employee or to remove any person therefrom.
I took the trouble to write some of the unions which have had difficulties in this connection and have secured some details of some of the problems with which they have had to deal. I wrote to the president of the confederation of national trade unions and I received a letter from the president, Mr. Jean Marchand who, as some members of the house will know, is now a member of the bi-culturalism commission. I want to read from the letter which he wrote me on March 23, 1964, and I quote:
We are in perfect agreement with this bill which aims to amend the Criminal Code so that the companies could not arbitrarily prevent their employees from joining a union. In the past, it was an accepted policy of the companies to forbid union organizers from visiting workers. Last year, we reached an agreement with the Quebec department of forestry so that passes are issued which entitle our organizers to travel freely on the companies' properties. But the system adopted is one based on privileges. We would prefer to have the Criminal Code amended and eventually the provincial laws.
We support your bill and we hope that it will get through.
I wrote to the international woodworkers of America and I received a letter from the vice president who wrote on behalf of their president on March 17, 1964. He cited a few examples of the difficulty which they had experienced, and I should like to read them into the record so members of the house will realize the type of problem which the union has had to face. I quote:
At Hystad Bros., Valemount, B.C., Canoe river camp, in March 1962, organizers Mike Sekora, R. E. Larson, and Ed Timmath were threatened by superintendent Jack Woods with R.C.M.P. action for trespassing. The superintendent told the employees in the bunkhouse that they had no right to invite a union man in to see them.
Industrial Lumber Ltd., Celeste, B.C., owned by Federated Co-operatives, organizers R. E. Larson and Clifford Michael were ordered out of the bunkhouse by Art Lloyd, manager of Federated Cooperatives, on the grounds of trespass.

All Fir Lumber Co. Ltd., McLeese Lake, B.C., organizer Ron Tweedie escorted out of bunkhouse by R.C.M.P. on the grounds of trespass.
North Western Pulp & Power Ltd., camp No. 2, Hinton, Alberta. In 1956, Frank Howard, M.P., and Michael Sekora, organizing for the I.W.A. were ordered out of the bunkhouse while signing up the crew. The superintendent, Stuart Allen, called local police to escort them from the property-the police did not respond because the local policeman happened to be an old I.W.A. member and a friend of Sekora.
I should like to cite some of the problems of the united steelworkers of America as they are set out in the "Miners' Voice" dated March, 1964. I quote:
Esterhazy, Sask.-Employees of International Minerals and Chemical Corporation (Canada) Limited who live in the trailer campsite here are being fenced in behind barbed wire and the camp has been declared by the company to be off bounds for visitors.
This latest move is another in a number of antiunion acts taken by I.M.C. to prevent union organization of its employees, charged representatives of the united steelworkers of America. That union is currently engaged in a membership drive at I.M.C. operations in nearby Yarbo.
Mr. Speaker, I am not proposing for a moment that anything be done to force workers to join a union. I believe workers have a right, under our law, to either join a union or not join a union. The point I am raising is that this provision in the Criminal Code dealing with trespass was never designed to be used to interfere with the rights of workers to join a union as it is being used now. This section of the Criminal Code, therefore, ought to be amended along the lines I have proposed. I want to cite some more cases which occurred in the province of Ontario. I shall quote from a letter which I received from the northern Ontario district council of lumber and saw mill workers unions. Here are some of the cases:
Henry Selin Forest Products-Hearst, Ontario.
Numerous attempts were made between 1946 and 1961 to get into the camp area which is seven miles off highway 11, 35 miles west of Hearst. All of these attempts failed. In the early part of 1961, the union repaired 14 miles of old winter haul road and went around the gate and into the camps with 35 organizers. At 3 a.m. a union organizer had to walk out to call the O.P.P. as Selin had blocked the road in many places with bulldozers, graders, trucks and trees. The union had over 90 per cent of the employees in the union when they came out. This shows the men wanted the union, and the union was subsequently certified by the labour relations board and had to pull a strike for a first agreement in October, 1961. Selin immediately blocked the road leaving 42 families isolated without food, medical care, etc. He barred these people from using the road. The union, at great expense, flew all the necessary supplies in to these people, and finally secured an injunction to open the road.
Criminal Code
Numerous small operators operate in the area of Chapleau, Ontario. All operate on crown land and all have so-called private roads. Some have gates, others have not.
In the year of 1963, the union had an invitation from the employers in Chapleau Lumber to organize them. This is partly a jackpot family camp and partly bunk-houses. There is no gate on the road. The union secured permission from management to visit the camp (subsequently, this was withdrawn) , when the organizers (five in number) went in, the operator called the O.P.P. and attempted to have them arrested for trespass. Charges of trespass were laid against the five and on a later occasion, on another visit, three more were charged wtih the same offence.
In my own province, Mr. Speaker, we have had the development of one of the largest industrial complexes at Thompson, Manitoba. Preparatory to building that plant it was necessary to build a power plant, which was built at Kelsey, some miles from Thompson; but despite the fact that it took two years to complete the building the trade unions were never able to get into that power plant project to discuss with the workers the advisability of their joining a union.
The only way to get into the area was by a spur line railway which was controlled by International Nickel, who instructed the C.N.R. not to sell tickets and not to permit anybody on a train except people with passes from the company. I have in my file sworn affidavits to prove that men worked on that project for as long as six months at a time, seven days a week, working as much as 100 hours a week, not because they wanted to but because they were told that unless they were prepared to work those hours they would be fired immediately.
Those men wanted to join unions, but during the entire time this project was being constructed they were unable to contact union people because the company used the provisions of the Criminal Code, which in my opinion were never meant to be used in this way to get around the very clear intent of the parliament of Canada which passed the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and of the provincial governments which passed labour relations acts.
In the same way, when the actual project was begun at Thompson, for two years or more it was impossible for any union organizer to get into Thompson. I know about this because as a member of the legislature I finally got them in, although I must say it took me close to three or four months to get through all the red tape and go from minister to minister, and from deputy minister to deputy minister, to try to get permission to meet the rules and the regulations.

Criminal Code
After I had done all this and had been turned down I went on. I told the company I would go in there whether the law permitted or not. I advised the company when I would go and suggested to them that they arrange with the R.C.M.P. to arrest me. I told them I was prepared to appear in court, that I would refuse to pay the fine, which was the only penalty that could be imposed, that I would then probably be adjudged to be in contempt of court, and if the company was prepared to stand the publicity of sending a member of the legislature to jail I was prepared to go to jail for whatever period the magistrate would assess.
But this is not a way which we can get good labour management relations. What we ought to do is amend this section of the code which has been used, is being used and will be used by some unscrupulous employers to get around the very clear intent of the labour relations act.
I hope hon. members of the house will not laud this bill to death, in other words that they will not talk it out. It may be that the government has not had enough time to consider all its implications, and I know it is not very often that a bill proposed by a private member is passed by the house. But if the government is not ready to permit passage of the bill today I would urge that it agree to send the bill to the industrial relations committee where representations could be made by the people concerned, by the unions which have had the difficulties I have mentioned- and there are other unions I have not mentioned which have had difficulties-and by employers who, if they have really good reasons which I have not mentioned for carrying on the kind of activities which I have outlined, could appear and give their reasons so that the committee could consider this matter thoroughly in all its aspects, and bring back a recommendation to the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I have to interrupt this exchange because the hon. member's time has expired, unless the house wants to give him unanimous agreement to continue

so that he may answer the question. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

Having looked at it, it is not very difficult to explain. The purpose of this bill is to permit legitimate action. The first 17 words permit a landlord to eject from his premises anybody who is, for example, having a wild party, creating a disturbance which bothers the other tenants, and so on. I think it is quite simple.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with much interest to the remarks made by the hon. member who spoke before me and even if he did labour his point, I doubt very much that the amendment he is submitting to the house would come under the administration of the Criminal Code.
It is clear and obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the provision he would add to section 41 of the Criminal Code is a provision essentially related to the labour code.
The Criminal Code in sections 40, 41 and 42, deals with the protection of movable property. There is first a provision for the protection of a dwelling house against breaking in or forcible entry.
There is also a provision for the defence not only of a dwelling house but also of real property against a trespasser.
There is also a provision for the assertion of right to real property by the person who is lawfully entitled, whether or not the owner claims a right.
Mr. Speaker, it is a question of establishing the right of the occupant. Is he an occupant by sufferance? Is he a tenant? Is he a landlord? It is advisable to set boundaries to know up to which point it is possible to resist the intrusion of another person. It is difficult to pass an amendment such as the one introduced because it contains many ambiguities.
It reads as follows:
(3) Except where a landlord would be therein justified under a covenant with a tenant for quiet enjoyment-
As pointed out a little earlier by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), that is when he asked a question to get more information, the beginning of this amendment leaves us wondering and makes it rather hard to understand its meaning.
The question is to find out if the landlord is ready to require his tenant to occupy the

rented premises according to the conditions set out in a lease. It such or such a condition is set out in a lease, the tenant has to comply with it, nothing more. There is no need to amend the Criminal Code to determine how the person who occupies the premises-that is whether the landlord is an employer or an employee, whatever his trade or profession-* must behave; the lessee must comply with the conditions set out in the lease.
If there is no lease, reference will be made to the civil code of the province where the lease is granted, in order to know, when it is a tacit lease, in which way it must be executed, under what conditions the tenant must occupy the leased premises. The Criminal Code is concerned when the question is to determine in which way someone must face an aggression, an attack or a trespass. If someone is attacked, he has the right, under the provisions of the Criminal Code, to defend himself. The conditions for admission of selfdefence are set out in sections 34 to 37 inclusive of the Criminal Code.
The conditions required to act in selfdefence are the following:
A person must be illegally assaulted, must not have provoked his attacker, must not have intended to kill or seriously injure him and must not have resorted to anything else but the necessary force.
When serious injuries have been inflicted or death occurred following the quarrel created, as it were, by resisting the aggression, then, the person alleging self-defence must have had reasons to fear either death or serious injuries, or fear, for reasonable motives, that he could not himself escape death or serious injuries.
That is the theory of legitimate defence.
The case mentioned by the hon. member could occur if, after allowing his employee to occupy a property he owns, an employer sought to prevent a third party from visiting his employee on the premises in question.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to the point which interests the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). All those things had to be explained to my hon. friend because he does not understand anything about the Criminal Code. He may be conversant with matters pertaining to labour conditions but the Criminal Code has a very distinct character, in that it contains provisions for the maintenance of public order and, in this case, for the protection, first, of the person and then of the individual's property, both real and movable.
Criminal Code
As I said a moment ago, the amendment now before us cannot be inserted in any way in the Criminal Code, because it is in no way related to the spirit which characterizes the Criminal Code.
As I have already pointed out, if a third party comes to meet or visit someone occupying his employer's property, the question is then to determine the right of the occupant, and that only in the light of the civil code. There is no question here of applying the Criminal Code. It is a matter of finding out what rights has the occupant of those premises, in what manner he is entitled to occupy those premises as provided in a written lease or one that is merely implied.
If the employer wishes to prevent the visitor or third party from going to the place occupied by the employee, everything depends on how he will go about it. If the employer assaults the visitor or the third party, then, the Criminal Code will provide protection for the employee or the visitor if the employer illegally commits an assault.
Therefore, there is no reason to amend the Criminal Code. We only have to establish the right of a tenant and to see to what extent, under the labour legislation, union organizations can authorize such relationship with union leaders and company employees.
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member introduces an amendment to the Criminal Code in order to determine the nature of relations between employer and employee, then, I say he goes the wrong way about it and he should merely see to it that labour legislation be amended accordingly.

I am very sympathetic to the objectives of the hon. member who introduced this bill to the house. We have gone a long way in our democratic society in providing access for the ordinary man, the worker, to organizations to protect himself against the overwhelming power of his employer within the framework of trade unions. Everyone in this house is sympathetic to the need for legislation to protect the rights of Canadian workers.
One wonders however in looking at this bill whether the hon. member has approached the question from the right side. Is he approaching something which belongs essentially to the realm of property law? Should he have brought this provision in by means of an amendment to the labour laws or by way of a resolution? I wish to comment on one or two points which came to my mind-

Criminal Code
and it is not a legal mind-as I read this bill and as I listened to the hon. member discussing it in the chamber today. I wonder how this measure would affect military property or, let us say, the army, where the army is the employer and where the employee is a soldier in a bunkhouse or a married soldier with a family living in married quarters on a national defence establishment. Would not the same law which he is proposing here essentially to deal with a labour matter apply in an area in which he had not anticipated it would apply?

Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the hon. member would permit a question.
I would be very glad to answer a question.

I am very sympathetic to labour organizations but I wonder whether the hon. member is suggesting that we should extend the rights of people to belong to a union so that the ordinary private in the army could belong to a union which would deal with his officers? Is that what the hon. member is suggesting?

I am afraid I was not suggesting that for a moment. I was suggesting that the hon. member has brought into the house a bill which deals with the relationship between landlord and tenant, and the landlord's rights in respect of that property. If this bill were passed by the house its provisions would apply equally in the case of national defence properties, and the relationship of members of the armed forces, as it would to the landlord and tenant relationship which he has explained may exist in mill towns, and for which he really wishes this bill passed by the house.
I suggest to the hon. member that there is a great deal of difference in the relationship of a landlord or an employer with regard to bunkhouses. This was raised in letters which the hon. member quoted. I believe that in a lumber camp, a fishing cannery, or whatever it may be, where temporary quarters are constructed some discipline must apply with regard to such temporary living quarters, and there really is no tenant and no lease in respect of these bunkhouses that applies to the particular case the hon. member has in mind.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this is really not the avenue through which to approach this problem, but that adequate avenues are open to the hon. member and he

would indeed be advancing the cause of labour were he to seek these avenues and bring his suggestion on to the floor of the house either through the labour laws or by way of a resolution for discussion by the house.
I have one further small point to raise after listening to my hon. friend. Under the legislation he proposes, a stranger would now have more right than a tenant in the very property in which the tenant lives. I say this because the tenant is bound by the terms of his lease, by the terms of the agreement with his landlord in regard to staying there; but the stranger who comes upon the property, under the bill of my hon. friend, could not be ejected and would indeed enjoy more freedom upon the property than the tenant himself. I do not think it was the aim of my hon. friend to bring about such a relationship when he introduced this bill.
In the early part of his discussion, in reply to a question which the hon. member answered I was not certain that the wording of this bill would prevent the committing of a nuisance on the property. I wonder whether the landlord would be able, under the wording the hon. member has given, to eject, let us say a bagpipes player who insisted on tucking the bag of his bagpipes under his arm and spanking out into action at twelve o'clock at night.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
I will be glad to answer a question.
Would the hon. member tell us what he has against bagpipes, which produce perhaps one of the finest types of music to be heard?
Is this a filibuster?

I have no objection to bagpipes, to pipe organs or to instruments of any kind, provided they are played quietly and at the proper time. But I think in a closely packed community there are limits in this regard and sometimes the landlord might have to take the necessary action to restrict the exuberance of even a bagpipes player.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
I am honoured, Mr. Speaker; I have never been asked so many questions. I must be doing very well today.
Does the hon. member not agree that the definition of bagpipes is an ill wind that nobody blows good?
No; that is the definition of an oboe.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Did you say "hobo" or "oboe"?

That is an oboe.
I think, Mr. Speaker, some of the examples I have given are enough to indicate that there are difficulties, and very obvious difficulties, in this bill. I suggest to my hon. friend that he would find a sympathetic audience everywhere in this house if he could find the means to achieve what he wants by way of legislation with which the house can deal.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up the remarks of previous speakers by pointing out that this is really a more appropriate provision for labour relations legislation under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act or, in the case of Thompson, Manitoba, to which the hon. member referred, the Manitoba labour relations act. I think the weakness of the hon. member's bill was perhaps best disclosed by the hon. member himself in reply to my question as to the meaning of the starting phrase of the bill:
Except where a landlord would be therein justified under a covenant with a tenant for quiet enjoyment-
The reply of the hon. member indicated that it was his impression that the covenant for quiet enjoyment was an obligation which required a tenant to use the property quietly. I would point out that the obligation of a covenant for quiet enjoyment is quite the reverse; it falls on the landlord and is not at all related to the purposes which to a layman like my hon. friend might appear to be most obvious. Perhaps I may refer my hon. friend to the work of a very distinguished Manitoban, the former chief justice of the court of Queen's bench, Hon. E. K. Williams. This work is entitled "Canadian Law of Landlord and Tenant", and I would refer my hon. friend to page 339 of that work, where he points out as follows:
The covenant for quiet enjoyment is an assurance against the consequences of a defective title and of any disturbance thereupon and of any substantial interference by the covenantor or those lawfully claiming under him with the enjoyment of the premises for all usual purposes.
Criminal Code
To restate it in perhaps less technical language, it is an undertaking either implied by law in the lease or included expressly in the lease to make it incumbent upon a landlord to ensure to his tenant, first that he is in fact the owner of the property he is purporting to lease, and the tenant will not be disturbed in it by adverse claims of ownership; and second, that the landlord will not by any act disturb the tenant in his enjoyment of the property. It is also pointed out by the learned author in the same edition of this work, at page 343:
In order to constitute a breach of covenant for quiet enjoyment, it is sufficient that the lessee's ordinary and lawful enjoyment of the demised land be substantially interfered with by the acts of the lessor, or those lawfully claiming under him, although neither the title to the land nor the possession thereof be otherwise affected.
I would point out that this gives to the tenant in question an obvious civil right which he can pursue in the civil courts of the province to protect him against the kind of harassment to which the hon. member has been referring. Specifically Mr. Speaker, it has been held in various cases that the tenant, the tenant's invitees, those coming in to engage in business relations with him, or the tenant's licencees-that is, those coming in for non-commercial reasons-are entitled to have access to the property, and actions of the landlord which would prevent such persons or the tenant from having the normal use of the property may be the subject of an injunction under the landlord and tenant act. It would appear-

I wonder whether I could ask the hon. member a question. How long does he think a worker in a camp who went to his employer and said "I should like Mr. Smith, the union organizer, to come and visit me" would be able to continue before he was fired?

speechtext: I am suggesting, and the hon. member merely underlines my argument again, that the proper course of action for him to take is not by producing garbled amendments to the Criminal Code but by producing amendments to the appropriate labour legislation, which essentially would-
Which you would talk out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let the hon. member bring forward an amendment to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and we will see.

Do you think we have not tried?

Criminal Code

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We have seen, and we know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member has no such legislation on the order paper and is in fact proceeding on a misunderstanding of the law applicable in these circumstances. What has to be borne in mind, as the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deach-man) pointed out so effectively, is that the effect of this particular provision would go far beyond the provisions relating to labour disputes which so much concern my hon. friend-and I do not for a moment question the legitimacy of his concern. First of all, the effect would be to prevent a landlord from taking action to expel a squatter, which is not connected with a labour dispute-someone with no colour of right to be on the land in question. Yet as my hon. friend pointed out, the amendment could apply in such a way as to protect someone who was a mere trespasser on the land with no rights whatever. It could apply far beyond the labour union situation. It could apply to the hon. member's own residence or the residence of any hon. member of this house.
I would also point out that the effect of the provision would also prevent a landlord or the person responsible for property on behalf of other occupants, such as a bunk-house, a rooming house, an apartment or otherwise, from taking action to expel undesirable persons, persons undesirable in the view of other occupants of the premises. For example, such person as the loudmouth, the lunatic, or the drunk who might be in a particular rooming house and causing concern and disturbance to others. Under the provisions of the hon. member's amendment such person could not in any legitimate way be removed from the premises.
I would also point out to the hon. member that there is a substantial protection for persons in the form of jeopardy to which he referred. Once again while the hon. member read a great many hortatory statements into the record, he did not give any indication whether he had taken any expert advice or whether there had been any legal proceedings to determine the assertion which he made.
In this connection I refer him to section 42 (3) of the Criminal Code, and for the benefit of the house I might be permitted to read it into the record:
Where a person
(a)	having peaceable possession of a dwelling house or real property under a claim of right, or
(b)	acting under the authority of a person who has peaceable possession of a dwelling house or

real property under a claim of right, assaults any person who is lawfully entitled to possession of it and who is entering it peaceably by day to take possession of it, for the purpose of preventing him from entering, the assault shall be deemed to be provoked by the person who is entering.
The effect of the provision, therefore, is to extend the justification provisions which are already provided by section 41 and the earlier provisions of section 42 of the Criminal Code to the person who has a colour of right to be on the property, to tenants, to tenants' licensees, to tenants' invitees, permitting them to resist efforts by the landlord or the person acting on the authority of the landlord to exclude them from the premises, or otherwise be forced to prevent them from remaining on the premises. I suggest that substantially the provisions provided by the Criminal Code already give this right.
The hon. member referred at length to the practices of the International Nickel Company at Thompson, Manitoba. I have discussed these matters with the hon. member for York-Scar-borough (Mr. Moreau), for example, who has himself, as has the hon. member, had experience with that particular situation. Perhaps I am out of order in referring to these but I think they bring into question other federal legislation and other lines of possible legal action which, had the hon. member for Winnipeg North and his associates done slightly more resourceful thinking, could have been followed up. For example, the hon. member referred to the actions of the C.N.R. in refusing to ticket people who did not have a pass issued by the company. The C.N.R. is, after all, a common carrier and the provisions of the Railway Act should be considered from the standpoint of taking action to prevent such misconduct. I do not condone for a moment the suggestion that union organizers should not be entitled to go on the property but I do suggest that this is not the proper type of legislation-this kind of garbled, ill-conceived and badly drawn legislation founded on a misunderstanding of the law-to best protect the rights either of the organizer or of the people who most desire the protection of the law so that they can carry on this very legitimate objective.
In closing, I might make reference to the fact that perhaps this is one of the most obscure provisions that has been introduced into this house for some time. Not only is obscurity created because of a misunderstanding of the law on the part of the hon. member, to which I have already referred, but up until the time the hon. member rose to his feet this house had not had the courtesy

Business of the House
of an explanation of the situation which the hon. member is trying to remedy, or an explanation of what was the purpose of the bill. I can understand that he did not have an opportunity to give this explanation when he introduced the bill, because it was introduced along with many others at the start of the session; but I do deplore the fact that the hon. member did not have the courtesy to put on the bill any explanatory note so that hon. members, and not just hon. members who may have some knowledge of the law of landlord or tenant or some knowledge of the law concerning labour relations, would know the specific problem to which the hon. member was directing himself and the effect of the provisions he is setting out. I would make these words applicable to all bills of this highly technical nature which are brought before the house. There is an obligation on hon. members to make a brief and lucid statement by way of explanatory note which is attached to the bill and serves to explain the purposes and objectives of it.
So, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the bill is founded on a mistaken knowledge of the law; that it would have application far beyond the field of labour relations to which the hon. member has sought to carry it; would have an adverse effect, as hon. members have pointed out, beyond the field
of labour relations; and because there are many incidental effects which the hon. member has apparently not foreseen, I would certainly oppose passage of this measure.
